en: The First Chapter of the *Chandoratnākara* composed by Ratnākaraśānti. Oṃ! Homage to Vāgīśvara.
Homage to the Victor, the sun among sages, whose nature is the supreme light; homage to him who creates day within the hearts of those who are bewildered in the night of inner darkness.
The Commentary on the *Chandoratnākara*.
Homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Lord of Speech!
To the Sage who, while remaining within the night, created the day within [the world].
And I pay homage to the Sun-like Jina, whose very self is the supreme light. ||1||
This treatise is composed specifically to provide a thorough understanding of one's own poetry and the poetry of others as they have been composed.
In this regard, Piṅgala [authored] the *Chandomūlasūtra*.
And Jayadeva has provided an illustration of that;
although it was composed by them, it is devoid of those eight qualities.
For example: therein, there is no condensation [of the rules] regarding the *prastāra* and so forth.
In matters such as the designations of light and heavy syllables, there is no metrical composition;
for the most part, it is merely indistinct,
and there is no arrangement of instructions for marvelous applications.
There is a mixture of the designations "ascetic" (*yati*) and "body" (*śarīra*), as well as "name" (*saṃjñā*) and "named" (*saṃjñin*), and there is also no simplicity.
For example: "In the *mayūrasāriṇī*, [the feet consist of] two *r* [gaṇas], then an *r* and a *g*. (| ' | ' | ' |)
The sequence of application [of the meters] is not as follows: "'vasujaladhivirāmau nau puṭā myau' and 'jātiścādidvāreṇa vibhaktā prācāṃ matā';
nor is it simple to recite 'vaitāliyaṃ rlganaidhanāḥ' and so forth."
The division of the pauses (yati) is also irregular; therefore, there is no pause at the end of a metrical foot (gaṇa).
Here, these eight qualities are also present.
Furthermore, there are also illustrative examples in the sūtras;
therefore, this [work] is the most excellent even among them.
Moreover, in this verse—
Clear, metrical, and concise, it is illustrated by aphorisms; its qualities are non-confusion, proper sequence, recitability, the use of syllabic groups (gaṇas), and appropriate pauses (yati). ||2||
A *padya* consists of four lines (*catuṣpadī*), and it is of two kinds according to the distinction between *vṛtta* and *jāti*:
*vṛtta* is measured by the number of syllables (*akṣara*), while *jāti* is measured by the number of morae (*mātrā*). (2)
"Verse (*padya*) consists of four lines.
That which is endowed with four lines is "four-lined" (*catuṣpadī*).
The word *pāda* refers to the four lines, or it is a collection of words; that which possesses these four lines is a verse.
"And that is of two kinds according to the distinction between *vṛtta* and *jāti*";
thus, by the distinction between *vṛtta* and *jāti*, that *padya* (verse) is of two kinds.
*Vṛtta* is that which is measured by the number of syllables (*akṣara*).
Number (*saṃkhyā*), however, is counting;
that which is counted by means of syllables (*akṣara*) is *vṛtta*. That which has the number of morae (*mātrā*) as its count is *jāti*.
That which is measured by its quantity is *jāti*.

A short vowel is light; at the ends of words, it is generally heavy if curved. It is also heavy when preceded by a consonant lacking a preceding vowel, as well as in the case of long and protracted vowels. (3)
That which is a single syllable pronounced clearly by itself is called a *svara* (vowel).
Briefly stated, it is of three kinds: short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*).
In that regard, the short vowel consists of one mātrā, and it is fivefold: a, i, u, ṛ, and lṛ.
The long vowel, however, consists of two mātrās.
And that [protracted vowel] is of eight kinds: ā, ī, ū, ṝ, lṝ, e, ai, o, au;
however, the *pluta* (prolated) vowel has three morae (*mātrā*), and it is indeed of nine kinds.
Just as eight long vowels are written, so too are eight protracted (pluta) vowels at the end;
the ninth is the single vowel *ḷ*,
which is not divided into three types.
Therefore, there are twenty-two vowels. That syllable which cannot be pronounced clearly by itself is a consonant (vyañjana).
From *ka* to *ha*, there are thirty-three.
Including the four— *anusvāra*, *visarga*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya*— there are thirty-seven in total.
Therefore, there are fifty-nine syllables in this treatise;
however, in the calculation of syllables, only the vowels (svara) are to be counted,
not the consonants (vyañjana).
For in this case, if there were a verse:
"The consonants are thirty-seven, and the vowel-letters are twenty-two;
these fifteen [consonants] are indeed counted by means of the vowels. (3)
"Laghurlṛjuḥ":
A short vowel becomes *laghu* and receives the designation *la*,
and it is straight (*ṛju*) in its depiction.
(For example: "sukṛtaklṛpti" (|| |||).
At the ends of words, a short vowel is generally long when followed by a consonant cluster (*guru*). At the ends of words, a short vowel is mostly long.
It becomes known as *gasaṃjña* (the *ga*-designation),
even when retrograde (*vakra*) in *Citrāṅka*;
why [is it said] "frequently" (*bahulam*)?
It does not occur in the *samā* [meters];
however, it occurs appropriately elsewhere at the ends of even feet.
But in the case of *indravajrā* and others, it may also occur at the ends of odd feet.
The syllable preceding a consonant that is itself devoid of a vowel is heavy, even if it is short; it is also called "crooked" (*vakra*). For example: *mṛtyuḥ kiṃ klṛpta* (◡ ◡ ◡ ◡ ◡).
Regarding "both the long and the prolated": the long and the prolated are always heavy and curved.
In dance and dress, they belong to women and gods. (‘ ‘ ‘ ‘ ‘ ‘ ‘ ‘ ‘) The prolated, however, is invariably light.
Indra and Agni have their syllables arranged as follows: (◡ ◡ ◡ ◡ | ◡ ◡ |).

A *tri* [foot] with the first syllable heavy is desired; likewise, one with the final syllable heavy (*jantaguru*), one with the middle syllable heavy (*santaguru*), and one where all syllables except the first are heavy (*māśeṣaguru*).

Furthermore, there is one with the first syllable light (*yādilaghu*), one with the second syllable light (*rantarlaghu*), and one with the third syllable light (*tantalaghu*), as well as one where all syllables except the last are light (*nāśeṣalaghu*). ||4||
A "bha" consists of three [morae] with the first being heavy;
that is, among three syllables,
that which has a heavy (guru) syllable at the beginning is desired as a "bha," and thus the designation "bha" is intended for it (||).

He is both the beginning and the teacher; thus he is the "original teacher" (ādiguru). Or, he is the teacher who is the very beginning. This should be understood in the same way for the others as well.
The "ja" [metre]: that which has a heavy syllable (guru) in the middle of three [syllables] is desired as being by its nature "ja"; it is considered to have the designation "ja" (| ' |).

That which has a long syllable at the end (*antaguru*)—namely, that which consists of three syllables—is desired as *satva*; this is the opinion. That which has no long syllable at the end (*aśeṣaguru*)—namely, that which consists of three syllables—is desired as *matva*.
The *gaṇa* known as 'ma' is (|||).
And that which begins with a short syllable (*yādi-laghu*)— that which has three syllables beginning with a short one— is the *ya* *gaṇa*.
It is accepted; that which is considered [to be so] is light at the end (*ratnalaghu*). When a group of three syllables has a light syllable at its end, it is the *ra* (*gaṇa*).
It is accepted; "ra" is considered [the second gaṇa].
It has a long syllable followed by a short syllable (ta-ta-la-gu).
That tri-syllabic group which has a long syllable followed by a short syllable is the "ta" (gaṇa).
It is accepted that "ata" is considered [the first *gaṇa*].
"Nā" is not entirely light. That which consists of three syllables and is entirely light is the "na" (*gaṇa*).
It is accepted; such is the view.
These are the eight. From three syllables come the *gaṇas*,
and they are indeed eight in number.
*bha*, *ja*, *sa*, *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *ta*, and *na*:
wherever these letters are restated (*anuvāda*), there the sūtras providing their respective designations (*saṃjñā*) should be recalled.
The first syllable heavy, the middle syllable heavy, the last syllable heavy, all syllables heavy;
the first syllable light, the penultimate syllable light, the third syllable light, all syllables light.
The meters are known through groups of six, with each subsequent one increasing by one syllable per foot:
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, and likewise Triṣṭubh.
"Chandas" is used for the purpose of defining the metrical structure.

Beginning with a foot consisting of six syllables, the meters are understood to be known by means of feet that increase by one syllable each thereafter. "Chandas" is the systematic arrangement of the sequence of meters.
Then, the designations of the meters are connected in sequence:
the *gāyatrī* has six syllables per foot;
the *uṣṇik* has seven syllables per foot.
The eight-syllable [verse] is the *anuṣṭubh*;
the nine-syllable is the *bṛhatī*;
the ten-syllable is the *paṅkti*.
The *triṣṭubh* has eleven syllables;
the *jagatī*, *śakvarī*, *aṣṭi*, and *dhṛti* each separately have one more [syllable] than the preceding;
and after the *kṛti*—which follows the *śuddhā*, *aprakṛti*, *samatī*, and *udgiti*—there are six, eight, and seven [syllables respectively]. (6)

The word *pṛthak* (separate) signifies each individual one. Any meter that follows the *triṣṭubh*, such as the *jagatī* and so forth, is designated as *atipara*, being separate—that is, each one individually.
A *jagatī* consists of twelve syllables;
a *atijagatī* consists of thirteen syllables.
The *śakvarī* consists of fourteen syllables;
the *ātiśakvarī* consists of fifteen syllables;
the *aṣṭi* consists of sixteen syllables.
The *atyāṣṭi* consists of seventeen syllables;
the *dhṛti* consists of eighteen syllables;
the *atidhṛti* consists of nineteen syllables.
Why was it stated separately for each? (Otherwise,) the designations *jagatī*, *śakvarī*, *aṣṭi*, and *dhṛti*—
as well as *ati-jagatī*, *ati-śakvarī*, *ati-aṣṭi*, and *ati-dhṛti*— would not occur in their respective order.
From this point onward, however, the meter is indeed *kṛti*, and the subsequent designations apply to the [feet] beginning with the first.
A *kṛti* consists of a foot of twenty syllables.
With twenty-one syllables it is *prakṛti*;
with twenty-two syllables it is *ākṛti*;
with twenty-three syllables it is *vikṛti*.
With twenty-four syllables it is *saṃkṛti*;
with twenty-five syllables it is *atikṛti*;
with twenty-six syllables it is *utkṛti*.
Thus, "six, eight, and horses" (ṣaḍaṣṭahayāḥ).
Those meters which have been declared by these three sūtras are, in their respective order, "six, eight, and horses";
for "horses" (haya) refers to seven.
However, number is indicated by means of objects whose numbers are already established;
therefore, "form" is one,
and "a pair" is two.
The fires are three; the Vedas and the oceans are four;
the arrows, the senses, and the objects are five.
The seasons and the flavors are six;
the worlds, the horses, the musical notes, and the sages are seven;
the Vasus and the delusions are eight.
The apertures and the planets are nine;
the directions are ten;
and the Rudras are eleven.
The Arka hymns are twelve;
the Bhava hymns are thirteen, and the Manu hymns are fourteen.

Metre is declared to be of three kinds: even (sama), half-even (ardhasama), and uneven (viṣama). These correspond respectively to the *tanumadhyā* class, the *upacitrakā* class, and the *vaktra* class. ||7||
Metre is said to be of three kinds: even (sama), half-even (ardhasama), and uneven (viṣama).
These, respectively, are exemplified by the *tanumadhyā* group, the *upacitrā* group, and the *vaktra* group.
Their "position" (*sthāna*) is determined by the presence of *yaga*, *ari*, and *riṣṭa* syllables at the end of the quarters.
The *bhādi* (meter beginning with *bha*) consists of *ta*, *va*, *nu*, *ti*, *bha*, *ādi*, *gva*, *lka*, one *ga*, and one *la* in each quarter-verse. ||8||
*Sthāna*, *yati*, *virāma*, and *sampat* are synonyms.
That which constitutes a pause (*sthāna*) by means of the desired syllables in both *vṛtta* and *jāti* meters is called *yati*—as in the example:
"gaṇḍasvedāpanayanarujāṃ klāntakarṇotpalānām."
"The rays from the nails of [his] feet are doubled by the moon-crested [Śiva] bowing down.
Why "by those who are dear"?
It would not apply to those who are not dear.
“This king is renowned, his fame is manifest;
by him, the masses of people are raised up by the banners of his army.
There shall be a pause (virāma) at the end of every foot.

The term "end" (anta) is carried over [from the previous rule]. It should be understood that the eight types of gaṇas beginning with *bha* are joined with a pause (*yati*) when an *u* sound occurs at the end. However, a heavy syllable (*guru*) joined with a pause is designated as *va*.
A light syllable joined with a pause (yati) is designated as *ka*.
These three sūtras are for the purpose of distinguishing between pauses based on symmetry.
Even common worldly usage, setting aside distinctions based on asymmetry of metrical feet (*gaṇa*), rests upon the distinction of symmetry.
One should practice the *yati* (caesura) at every foot;
this section concerns even meters (*samavṛtta*).
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Chandoratnākara* by the venerable Ratnākaraśānti.
The second chapter:
If there are *ta* and *ya*, it is *tanumadhyā*. (1)
If the syllables *ta* and *ya* were to occur in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), then it would be the meter named *tanumadhyā*.
In this treatise, the aphorism (*sūtra*) itself serves as the illustration;
therefore, the metrical expansion (*prastāra*) must be performed using the very letters of the aphorism.
(As in: "If *tyau* [occur], O slender-waisted one")—the phrase "if *tyau*" refers to the body (*śarīra*).
There is a pause (*yati*) at the ends of the metrical feet.
The phrase "by their feet" is to be connected with each quarter-verse (*pāda*).
"Tanumadhyā" is the name [of this meter]. The same should be understood for the others as well.
In verses with equal feet, one should compose the *padya* by applying the words of the *sūtra* four times;
the *kumāralalitā* consists of *jsaug*. ||2||
If *ja*, *sa*, and *ga* should occur in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), then the meter is called *kumāralalitā*. *Kumāralalitā* consists of *ja*, *sa*, and *ga*.
For this [syllable] *glau* is indeed common to all four. ||3||
That meter in which *ga* and *la* are fixed four times at every quarter-verse is indeed *samānī*;
and *glau* is *tuḥsā*, while *mānyasauhi*.
Thus, it possesses four means of valid cognition. ||4||
That [meter] in which a *la* and a *ga* occur four times at every foot is *pramāṇī*;
it is *pramāṇī* when there are four *la*s and one *ga*.
If it has the *bh*, *au*, and two *g*s, it is *citrapadā*.
If there are *bha*, *u*, and *ga* in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), then it is *citrapadā*; *citrapadā* occurs when there are *bha*, *u*, and *ga*.
If it consists of two *ma*s and two *ga*s, that is the *vidyunmālā* meter. ||6||
If there are two *ma*s and two *g*s in each quarter,
then it is *vidyunmālā*.
If there is a *ma* at the end of the *ga*, it is the *Avidyunmālā* [meter].
The *maṇḍapaka* [is formed] by adding the syllable *bhātta*. ||7||
If, in each quarter-verse, there are *bha*,
*ta*, *ga*, *la*, *gu*, and *ru*, then it would be the *māṇavaka* meter.
Piṅgala, however, has stated the *māṇavakākrīḍitaka* [meter].
The pupils struck the young student.
If it is *halamukhī*, then *rānna* [is the result]. ||8||
If, after the *rā* (ra-gaṇa) in each quarter, there should be *na* and *sa*, then it would be the *halamukhī*.
If she, whose face is like the moon, is here, O King.
The *bhujagaśiśu* meter consists of the ganas *na*, *ma*, *u*, *ma*, and *sa*. ||9||
If there should be *na*, *ma*, and *sa* in each quarter, then it would be the *bhujagaśiśusutā*.
We bow to Him who is in the form of a young serpent.
The Śuddhavirāj metre is known to have the syllabic pattern ma-sa-jaga (ma, sa, ja, ga). ||10||
If, in each quarter, there should be the syllables *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*, then it is to be known as *śuddhavirāṭ*.
The object of knowledge is the pure, supreme, and immortal essence.
Indeed, when there is a *ga* following *ma* and *na*, it is known as *paṇava*. ||11||
If, in each quarter-verse, there were a *ga* following the *ma-na-ya*s, then it is known as the *paṇava*.
A *gaṇa* consisting of four *ma*s and one *na* is indeed known as *paṇava*.
The Mayūrasāriṇī meter consists of the ganas ra, ja, and two gas (ra-ja-ga-ga). ||12||
If there should be *ra*, *ja*, *ra*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*) in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), then it would be *mayūrāsāriṇī*.
The Mayūrasāriṇī meter consists of the syllables sa, ya, ra, ja, ra, ga, and ga.
That [meter] is Rukmavatī where there are *sa*, *ga*, *ma*, *sa*, and *ga* in the even [pādas]. ||13||
That [meter] in which there are *bha*, *ma*, *sa*, and *ga* in each quarter-verse is called *rukmavatī*.
The two cows with golden-colored udders wandered about.
The *mattā* meter is to be known as composed of *ma*, *bha*, *sa*, *ga*, and *sa*. ||14||
Matta is to be known as that which is created by the gaṇas ma, bha, sa, and ga in each quarter.
It should be known as created by the one who is free from the darkness of the knowable.
From that, this Gāyatrī meter would be established. ||15||
If there were two *ta*s, followed by a *ja* and a *ga*, at the end of each quarter-verse (*pāda*), then it would be the *upasthitā*.
That [state] would be present as the third stage.
It would be Indravajrā if it consists of ta, ta, ja, ga, and ga. ||16||
If in each quarter there are *ta*,
*ja*, *ga*, and *ga*, then it is *indravajrā*.
O Indra, may there be [strength] for the thunderbolt; O you of vast power, may the cow be [granted].
For the Upendravajrā consists of the sequence ja-ta-ja-ga-ga. ||17||
If there should be *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and two *ga*s in each quarter, it is indeed *upendravajrā*.
Upendra, with the thunderbolt, whose vital energy is born from the *ga* and *au* vowels.

Those verses whose first two quarters possess the characteristics just described and consist of various metrical variations, and whose final two quarters are both characterized by smoothness and *yati*, are known as *upajātis* by the masters of tradition. (18)

When the two feet previously described for Indravajrā and Upendravajrā are combined, and both subsequent feet that follow them are likewise endowed with pleasing pauses (*yati*) and metrical elaboration (*prapañca*), those are known as *upajātis* by the masters of memory. How so?
"By various fourteen-fold conceptualizations" means that in both feet, as appropriate, the second and third [syllables] appear in the same position as the first; furthermore,
the interval between the four feet also exists within the initial syllables.
Therefore, it should be viewed as having been expanded like a four-syllable meter:
*indravajrā* above, *upendravajrā* below, and in the middle the fourteen *upajāti*s.
He [the author] desires *dodhaka* to consist of three *bha*s followed by *ga* and *u*. (19)
If there are two *ga* syllables after three *bha*s in each quarter-verse, then the sage desires that to be *dodhaka*. He desires *dodhaka* [when] after three *bha*s there are two *ga*s.
Or else, it is the Śālinī meter with two *ra* gaṇas and one *śa* gaṇa, according to the Veda and the world.
If there is the syllable *ma* joined with *va* at every foot, and two *ra*s also joined with *va*, with a pause (*yati*) occurring at the fourth and seventh syllables,
then it is *śālinī*.
*Mo-vā-rau-bā śālinī vedalokaiḥ*.
By the phrase "or the guru," the designation for a guru joined with a *yati* (caesura) is established.
If that is so, since the *yati* has already been indicated by the [rules on] Vedas and worldly [verse], for what purpose are these two [sūtras]? They are for the sake of clarification. [The rule is:
"If *ma*, *va*, *va*, or *stra* [occur], it is the *vātormimālā*. (21)
If in each quarter there is a *ma* (mātrā) followed by a *va*,
and likewise a *sa* and a *ra* followed by a *va*, with the pause (*yati*) occurring according to the Vedic and worldly conventions,
then it is the *vātormimālā*.
Jayadeva speaks of the *vātormī*: it consists of two *ma*s and two *ya*s, or else a garland of *tormi*s;
or it consists of a *ma*, a *va*, a *na*, and a *u*, which is the *bhramaravilasitā*. (22)

If there is a *ma* and a *va* together in each quarter, followed by a *na* and a *va* together, with the pause (*yati*) occurring according to the Vedic and worldly rules, then it is the *bhramaravilasitā*.
The movements of the bee are playful.
The Rathoddhatā consists of two *ra*s, one *la*, and one *ga*. ||23||
The Vedaloka meters are now concluded.
If there are *ra*, *na*, *ra*, *la*, and *ga* in each quarter-verse (*pāda*), then it is *Rathoddhatā*: "If *ra* is followed by *na*, *ra*, *la*, *ga*, it is *Rathoddhatā*."
The *svāgatā* consists of two *ratnabhaga* gaṇas and a heavy syllable (*guru*). ||24||
The *svāgatā* meter consists of the gaṇas ra, na, bha, and a heavy syllable (guru) in each quarter.
The Svāgatā metre consists of ra, na, bha, ga, ga, and a guru.
And it becomes the Vṛtta meter when there are na, na, sa, and ga, followed by gi. ||25||
If in each quarter there were *na*, *na*, *sa*, and *ga*, it would be the *vṛttā* meter;
likewise, if it were *na*, *na*, *sa*, *ga*, *ga*, it would be the *vṛttā* meter.
Na, na, ra, la, gi, and ca—these indeed constitute the Bhadrikā meter. ||26||
If in each quarter there are *na*, *u*, *ra*, a short (*laghu*) syllable, and a long (*guru*) syllable,
it is *bhadrikā*; likewise, *nanara* followed by *la* and *gi* constitutes *bhadrikā*.
In the Śyenī meter, there is a ra-gaṇa, a la-gaṇa, another ra-gaṇa, and a long syllable (guru) at the end. ||27||
If each quarter-verse consists of ra, ja, ra, a short syllable (laghu), and a long syllable (guru), then it is called Śyena.
The Śyenī meter consists of two *udīritas*, followed by *jau*, *ralau*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*).
And *jasau*, *ta*, *ga*, and *gā* would constitute the *upasthiti* metre. ||28||
If, in each quarter-verse, there should be *ja*, *sa*, *ta*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), then it would be the *upasthiti* [meter].
There would be impurity for ten days, and there would be the presence of the *upasthiti* [rite].
They traverse the lunar path with the dust of battle. || 29 ||
That path where *ra*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* syllables move at every foot is called the *candravartman*.
Moving like the moon through the paths of the sky.
They maintain that this *vaṃśastha* consists of the syllables *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and *ra*. (30)
That [meter] in which there are *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and *ra* in each quarter-verse is called *vaṃśastha*.
The Vaṃśastha meter is desired [to consist of] ma, ja, ta, and two jas.
It would indeed be an Indrivaṃśā where those two [syllables] are followed by two *jar* (long) syllables. ||31||
That [meter] in which there are *ta*, *ja*, and *ra* in each quarter-verse is indeed the Indravaṃśā;
it is the Indravaṃśā where *ta*, *ja*, and *ra* occur.
Puṭa, iha, vasu, vedā, nau, gava, urvau. ||32||
If, in each quarter-verse, there should be *na*, *u*, *ga*, *va*, *ra*,
and *va* (with a pause at the third and sixth syllables), and likewise *va*, *sa*, and *u* (with a pause at the fourth and seventh syllables); [this is the *Vasantatilakā*].
That, however, is the *puṭacchandas* here.
Puṭai havasu vedā naugavau rvauṃ.

"Yugma," "yugya," and "sama" are synonyms;
"ayugma," "ayuga," and "viṣama" are synonyms. They call the *upacitraka* that which has an odd number of *yati*s.
If there are thirty-one *salaga*s and three *gau*s. ||1||
If in the odd feet (the first and third) there should be *sa*,
*sa*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*);
And when there are three *bha* gaṇas in both even feet, followed by two *ga* gaṇas,
then they call that the *upacitraka* metre. (For example— )
In the case of half-equal meters (*ardhasama*), because they consist of half-measures, the verse should be constructed by repeating [the definition] twice.
If there are three *bha*s followed by a *ga*, it is *drutamadhyā*; if, however, there are *na*, *ja*, and two *ja*s, it is likewise [the same]. (2)
If, in the odd feet, there are three *bha* gaṇas followed by two heavy syllables (*guru*),
and if, in the even feet, there are *na*, *ja*, *ja*, and *ya* [gaṇas], [it is the Vaitālīya meter].
If it consists of three *sat* [laghu] syllables followed by a *guru*, it is *drutamadhyā*;
if there is a *ga* [guru] after three *bha* [bhagaṇa] syllables, it is *vegavatī*.
If there are three *sa*s followed by a *guru* in the odd feet,
and if there are two *bha*s followed by two *gurūs* in the even feet, then it is the *vegavatī* meter.
In that [meter], the odd [feet] consist of ta, ja, ra, pha, and ga; the even [feet] are the Bhadravirāj, consisting of ma, sa, ja, ga, and ga.
In which [meter], there are *ta*, *ja*, *ra*,
and *ga* in the odd feet, and *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga* in the even feet.
And when there are [these] gaṇas,
it is the Bhadravirāḍ; if there is an uneven [meter] with sa, ja, sa, and ga, it is the Sama.
In the *ketuvatī* [meter], there are *bha*, *ra*, *pha*, *na*, *ga*, and *ga*. ||5||
If there are *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *ga* in the odd feet,
and *bha*, *ra*, [and *na*] in the even feet, [it is the Vaitālīya meter].
If the [feet] consist of *na*,
*ga*, *ru*, and *ga*, it is *ketuvatī*. It would be *ākhyānikā* if those two [syllables] are *ja* and *ga*.
But in the *yuk* [meter], *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and two *ga*s are the feet. ||6||

If in the odd feet (the first and third) there are *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and a heavy syllable (*ga*), and in the even feet (*ta*, *ta*, *ja*, *ta*), there are *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and a heavy syllable (*ga*); [then it is the Vaitālīya meter].
When there are *ja*, *ga*, and *guru* [syllables], then it is the *ākhyānikā*.
It would be an Ākhyānikā if it has those two [gaṇas] followed by ja, ga, and ā;
that Ākhyānikā is one whose first part is reversed. ||7||
In which [meter], the odd feet consist of ja, ta,
ja, ga, and ga;
If, however, in both even feet, those two (ja and ga) along with a long syllable (guru) occur, that is called Ākhyānikā with the first [foot] reversed.
If there are three *sagaṇas*, followed by a *laghu* and a *guru*, and then six *gaṇas* consisting of *nagas* (three *laghus*) and a *bha* (*ragaṇa*), it is then called *hariṇaplutā*. 8.
If there is a short syllable followed by a long syllable after three *sa*s in the odd feet, and *na*, *bha*, *bha* in the even feet,
[it is the Vaitālīya meter].
If there are *ra* and *sa*,
it is the *hariṇaplutā*; if there are *na*, *na*, *ra*, *la*, *ga*, *na*, *ja*, and *ja*, [it is the same].
And if, at that time, it is intended as the *aparavaktra* [meter], [then it is so]. ||9||
If there are *na*, *na*, *ra*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*) in the odd feet,
and *na* in the even feet;
When *jaḥ*, *ja*, and *raḥ* occur,
then it is desired as *aparavaktra*.
If there are *ya*, *yu*, *ga*, *i*, *ha*, and if *na*, *u*, *ra*, *ya*, *ca*, *yu*, *gma*, *na*, *ja*, *ja*, *ra*, *ga* follow, they call it *puṣpitāgra*. 10.
The word *iha* refers to the *ārddhasama* meters. If, in the odd quarters, there should be *na*, *na*, *ra*, and *ya*;
And in our even feet, there are *ja*,
*ja*, *ra*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*).
Then they call it *puṣpitāgrā*.
These two are varieties of *vaitālīya*:
*repha-ja-ra-ja*, as well as *ja-ra-ja* and *ja-ra-ga*.
The suffix *matup* is used in the feminine gender up to the point where it shares the same designation as the base word.
If there are two *ra*s in the odd feet,
and *ja*, *ra*, *ja*, *ra* in the even feet, [it is the Vaitālīya meter].
And if they should be heavy, then it is "yavamatī.
Since the word *yava* takes the suffix *matup*, that which is denoted by it is prescribed specifically for the feminine; thus the meaning is "yavamatī" (possessing barley).

If the odd [pādas] consist of ten, ten, and two light syllables, and the other [even pādas] likewise consist of ten, ten, and ten light syllables, with a heavy syllable at the end—provided that both have an arrangement of charmingly measured feet—it is the Śikhā metre. (12)
If there are twenty-eight light syllables in the odd feet and thirty light syllables in the even feet,
and if both [feet] end in a heavy syllable, it is the *lalitapadavisṛti*.

Then it becomes the *aśikhā* [meter]. With its construction of petals formed by the exchange of its own abodes as expressed by even and uneven feet, this [meter] here in the world invariably bears the name "shackle for binding the crooked. (13)
That position which is described as being fixed by both even and uneven [feet] is devoid of restriction;
where the arrangement of half-[verses] is reversed, this is known here in the world as *nigaḍita* (the fettered).
A person with crooked feet, however, is likewise known as *nigaḍita*.
Likewise, for that whose designation is a corresponding name, the meaning is "binding in this manner.
[This concludes] the *ardhasama* meters.
The Fourth Chapter:
That meter in which there is no equality of heavy and light syllables, or equality of phonemes, across all four feet is called *viṣama* (irregular).
It is of four types: *vaktra*, *caturūrdhva*, *udgatā*, and *pracupita*.
In verses consisting of eight syllables per quarter, one should not take *snau* (the ganas sa and na) as the opening, for it is the mouth of the ocean.
Excluding the first and the last, this is the *vaktra* variety of the *prastāra* known as "twice the middle" (*dviguṇamadhyākhya*).
If the quarters (*pāda*) consist of eight syllables,
then even there, provided there is no *sn* after the first syllable, if a *ya* occurs after the fourth [syllable], it is *vaktra*.
The first half-verse is indeed the previous sūtra;
therefore, by repeating it twice, the verse is to be completed. When there is the letter *ja* in the even quarters, it is celebrated as the *vaktra* meter. ||2||
The opening is called *pathyā*;
what is its specific distinction?
It is that, after the ocean (the fourth syllable) of the even quarters, there is the letter *ja*.
This [type of *viparīta*] has been described as occurring between two *jenāyuja* [pādas]; it does not occur here [in this case].
That which is wholesome (pathyā) becomes unwholesome (viparītapathyā) when reversed; this is the meaning. Here, the "mouth" (vaktra) is cited as an example of the *viparītapathyā*.
What is the distinction [between them]?
In the odd pādas, after the syllable *ja*, there is *ambudhi* (four mātrās);
that same [opening] with the syllable *na* in the odd pādas should be known as *capalā*. (4)
That same [meter] is to be known as Capalā;
if one asks what the distinction is,
it is that after the ocean (four) syllables in the uneven quarters, there is an *n*.
That [verse] in which the seventh and the pair [of the fifth and sixth syllables] are short is considered by the Sage to be the Vipulā. ||5||
That very same *vaktra* meter, in which the seventh syllable of both feet is light, is considered *vipulā* by the sage Piṅgala;
it remains that same [meter] for him in every respect.
In this *vaktra* meter, wherever there is a light syllable as the seventh in every foot, that is considered by that teacher to be *vipulā*.
Beyond this, the verse should be composed by repeating [the pattern] four times; by the *bha* [gaṇa], it is *ambudhi-vipulā*. (7)
When the sign following the mouth of the ocean (the face of the ocean) is present, that is the meaning of "vipulā";
and by means of the letter *ra*, it is likewise [formed] from what follows that. 8.
In every instance of the *vaktra* meter, after the syllable *ra*, there should be another [syllable] different from it;
thus, that *vipulā* is a *rakāravipulā* (or *ravipulā*). It is likewise with the syllable *na*. (9)
When the syllable *na* occurs everywhere in the opening (*vaktra*) of the *ambudhi* meter, it is the *vipulā* known as *nakāra-vipulā* (or *navipulā*).
Likewise, it may also occur with the syllable *ta*. ||10||
In every instance of the *vaktra* meter, that [same] *vipulā* which follows after the syllable *ta* is called *takāra-vipulā* (or *tavipulā*).
It is likewise seen following after the syllable *ma*. (11)
When it occurs everywhere in the opening (vaktre) of the ocean (ambudheḥ), even with the letter *ma*, that is seen as the *makāra-vipulā*;
anything other than this is indeed the *vitāna*.
Whatever other characteristic of the *vaktra* meter is mentioned besides the one already cited,
all of it constitutes the *vitāna*.
[In the *vitāna*,] there are *sa* and *na* at the beginning of all feet, and *ja* and *mbu* (ma-bha) in the even feet.
"In the case of uneven [pādas], it should be as beautiful as possible"—this is generally how one observes their application. 13.
Regarding those varieties of Vaktra that have been described, poets should generally observe similar applications for them in brief:

thus, in all quarters (pādas), there are no *s* or *n* syllables following the initial letter; and in the odd-numbered quarters, there shall be a *j* syllable following the "ocean" (*ambu-dhi*, i.e., the fourth syllable).
In the odd feet, after the *ambudhi* (four) gaṇas, there should be *bha*, *ra*, *na*, *ta*, or *ma*;
the remainder may be anything else as it pleases.
The Differentiation of Faces.

The first foot consists of eight syllables, and each subsequent one increases by four from the preceding; that which possesses this [structure], beautified by various arrangements, is [the Vaitālīya].
The wise declare that the *padacaturūrdhva* meter possesses a path of gracefully elegant words. ||14||
That meter which has eight syllables in its first quarter, and each subsequent quarter increases by four syllables respectively,
being thus beautiful through its various arrangements and possessing a charming path of words, the wise call that indeed the *viṣama* (irregular) *caturūrdhva*.
Its feet should also be understood from the *jāti* and *vṛtti* meters according to their constituent parts (*aṅga-gaṇa*).
For example: the first [foot] is like the first foot of the *sūtra* meter; the second is like the second foot of the *āryā*; and the third and fourth are like the second half-verse of the *āryā*.
In the *padacaturūrdhva* meter, there is a *prastāra* consisting of four [syllables per line];
here, in this *padacaturūrdhva*, the first [line] consists of eight syllables.
If all the light syllables are in the *gagana* (the first quarter),
and it brings joy to the world when joined with the prefix *āṅ*, then it becomes the *pīḍa* metre, provided it possesses gracefully elegant pauses and movements. ||15||
In this context, within the *padacaturūrdhva* class itself, that [meter] in which there are two heavy syllables (*guru*) at the end of each quarter and all others are light,
and where the movement of the cadence is endowed with graceful grace (*salalita-yati-gati*), brings forth joy because it is of such a nature;
however, when joined with the prefix *ā*, it becomes *pīḍa*.
The meaning is that even then it remains unafflicted.
If the first foot here falls near [the end of the previous line], it is the *caraṇa*.

When one [of the three] dwells in the midst of another's residence while being attended by others, whereas the other two remain in their own unshakable abodes, this is the *kalikā* [arrangement]. ||16||

In this case, if the first quarter-verse (pāda) is indeed an *āpīḍa*, and having passed over the second quarter-verse, it does not further exceed the limit of the next [quarter] but dwells in the middle itself,
then the other three quarters dwell in their own respective abodes.
Such indeed would be the *kalikā*,
if the pair of feet is very close together and the first foot here falls evenly [upon them].
The triad of the other feet remains in its own unshakable abode; such is the graceful play of the *lava* meter. 17.

The first quarter remains exactly as in the *āpīḍa* meter; if it exceeds the second quarter by three [mātrās], while the other two quarters remain exactly as they were, then it becomes the *lavalīlā*.
The other three quarters remain entirely unchanged.
If the first foot here falls into a *sam* [meter],
it is certainly a stream of nectar that generates delight through its various prescribed and graceful cadences (*yati*). 18.

If the first quarter of an *āpīḍa* indeed consists of three feet situated in their own respective positions, and it produces delight through well-arranged graceful pauses (*laya*), then it certainly becomes a stream of nectar.
Varieties of the *padacaturūrdhva* meter.
If first there are *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *la*s,

followed immediately by *na*, *sa*, *ja*, *ga*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), and then, after two short syllables (*atha-ūh*), there are *bha*, *na*, *ja*, *la*, and *ga*s; [then it is the Vasantatilakā meter].
This [meter] is called Udgatā when it consists of sa, ja, sa, and ja gaṇas. ||19||
If, in the first [foot], there should be *ja*, *sa*, *sa*, and *laghu*;
immediately after that, in the second, *na*, *sa*, *ja*, and *guru*;
and then, in the third, *bha*, *na*, *ja*, *la*, and *ga*—[this constitutes the *Viyoginī*].
Furthermore, in the fourth [foot], there should be *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*; thus, this is the *udgatā*. Indeed, three [feet] are exactly like the *udgatā*, while the third is otherwise.
It is known that this fragrance, strung together with the divisions of the *rana* ornaments, they describe as being of such a kind. ||20||
Where the three feet other than the third are identical to the *udgatā*,
but the third foot is known to be otherwise—
how so? For the third [foot] is composed of *ra*, *na*, *bha*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), whereas the others are otherwise.
When there is a triplet of these two [syllables] followed by *sa* and *ya* in the third quarter, it is the *lalita* metre due to its gracefully extended arrangement of feet.
For that which is desired by poets is indeed called *lalita* (the graceful). ||21||
Where the third quarter consists of *na*, *u*, and *sa*, and the remaining quarters are similar to those of the *udgatā*,
that is indeed desired by poets as *lalita*.
Because it is charming through its spreading arrangement of words,
it belongs to the *udgatā* class of meters.

If in the first quarter there are *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, *bha*, and two *gurus*, and then *sa*, *na*, *ja*, *ra*, *ga*, followed by *na* and *sa*; and then *na*, *yu*, *ta*, *na*, *na*, *ja*, *ya*, [that is the Vamśasthavila].
This *pracupita* meter is declared to have been previously established. ||22||
If in the first quarter there are *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, *bha*, and two heavy syllables (*guru*), then [the second quarter] is as follows:
if in the second there are *sa*, *na*, *ja*, *ra*, and a heavy syllable;
and in the third, "furthermore" (*param*), there are *na*, *na*, and *sa*.
Now, "atha" refers to the fourth [chapter], where there is no *traya*.
When *ja*, *ya*, and this [same sequence] occur together in one place, it becomes *Upasthitapracupita*.
If in a quarter (*pāda*) there are *na*, *u*, *sa*, *na*, *na*, and *sa* in the third [foot].
Poets call that the Vardhamāna;
here, another [meter] exists which is similar to the Pracupita, possessing the entire arrangement of characteristics for each fixed quarter-verse. ||23||
If in the third foot there should be *na*, *na*, *sa*, *na*, *na*, and *sa*, and if here too the rule for all other feet is prescribed as being similar to that of the *pracupita*,
then poets call it *vardhamāna*.
When there is a pause after the third and first syllables in this [meter], they call it Ārṣabha;
that is a specific variety of Śuddhavirāj.
If there is a subsequent triad equal to the *pracupita* meter, [it is called *vaitālīya*]. ||24||
When the third foot consists of *ta*, *ja*, and *ra*, and there is a pause (*yati*) after its first syllable;
If its third foot were identical to the *pracupita* gaṇa, then that specific type of *śuddhavirāj* is called by the name *ārṣabha*; they call that *vṛtta* "Śuddhavirāḍ-ārṣabha.
These are the varieties of *pracupita*.
Fifth Chapter. The varieties of *vṛtta* have been declared; from here onwards, the *jāti*s must be explained.
A short syllable (*laghu*) consists of one *mātrā*, while a long syllable (*guru*) consists of two.
The varieties of *vṛtti* have been explained; now the *jāti*s must be described.
*Jāti* is also of three kinds: the *āryā*,...

Vaitālīya and Mātrāsamaka. Among these, Āryā, which exceeds [the standard] by three morae, resembles the uneven meters (viṣamavṛtta), while Vaitālīya, which exceeds [the standard] by two morae, resembles the half-even meters (ardhasamavṛtta).

The *mātrāsamaka* meter, which is distinct from the three types of vertical meters (*ūrdhvatraya*), resembles a symmetrical meter (*samavṛtta*). In this class [of meters], the calculation is by *mātrās* and not by consonants; however, one short syllable (*laghu*) constitutes one *mātrā*.
With one *guru* there are two *mātrās*.
Five *bhajasas*, a pair of *gurus*, and four *laghus* constitute the *gaṇas* of four *mātrās*.
Among them, *ca* and *kha* consist of four *laghus*; *ka* consists of one *mātrā*; and *da* consists of two *mātrās*. (2)
Among the groups of four morae, there are the *bha* group, the *ja* group, and the *sa* group.
There are two *gurus* and four *laghus*, making five;
these five groups are also designated by the term *casa*. Among the groups, the fifth consists of four *laghus*.
That [syllable] is designated as *kha* and also as *ca*;
however, a *gaṇa* consisting of a single *mātrā* is designated as *ka*.

The *dvimātraka* is called *da*; it is of two kinds: either two short syllables (*laghu*) or a single long syllable (*guru*). If, in the odd positions, there are eight *gaṇas* in each half-verse (*dala*) excluding the *ja* *gaṇa*, it is an *āryā*.
In the latter half, the sixth letter is *ka*, the eighth is *da*, and in both cases the remaining letters are *a*. (3)
If there are eight *gaṇas* in both halves [of the verse], then it is an *āryā*.
How are there eight?
By excluding the letter *ja* from the odd positions—the first, third, fifth, and seventh.
In that regard, having combined the sixth gaṇa into a single mātrā in the latter half, there are two mātrās in the eighth gaṇa of both halves,
while the remaining gaṇas consist of four mātrās each. There is no light (laghu) syllable in the eighth position.
Because of the heaviness at the end of the half-verse:

in the first half, the sixth syllable is either *ja* or *kha*, provided there is no light syllable following it; the pause (*yati*) occurs after the sixth syllable, or if followed by *kha*, it occurs at the end, or even at the fourth syllable in the latter half. (4)
In the first half [of the verse], the sixth *gaṇa* should be made with the letter *ja*, as in the previous rule;
or else, it should be with the letter *kha*, as in this present rule.
When the sixth [syllable] of the first half would be *kha*, [the rule applies].
In that case, however, the pause (yati) should be made at the first light syllable,
provided that the sixth gaṇa in the first half-verse also has a *kha* following it;
"having a *kha* after it" (*khapara*) means that which has a *kha* as its subsequent element.
Then it is the sixth;
at its end, a pause (yati) should be made.
That which has a pause at the end is called "antayati."
If, in the final syllable-leaf (pada), in its latter half, the fourth gaṇa should be "khapara" (consonant followed by a short vowel),
and by the word "api" it may also be the sixth [gaṇa],
then a pause (yati) must also be made at the end.
Therefore, the group of one mātrā is beautiful.
In one place, because of the word "ending in the nominative singular" (*prathamanta-vat*), it consists of that [suffix].
For this very reason, in the first half, the sixth is indeed *kha*.
The pause (yati) occurs at the beginning of the sixth [syllable];
in the seventh, there is a pause only after *kha* when followed by a sixth [syllable],
and in the latter half, there is a pause only after the fifth *kha*.
The pause occurs after the fourth [syllable], and the seventh is indeed a *kha*;
the pause occurs after the sixth—this is the definition for all pauses (*yati*).
The example, however, is the sūtra itself.
When both uneven feet are completed by those three [gaṇas], then it is *pathyā*; but if even one [of them] is not concluded by those uneven [gaṇas], then it is *vipulā*. 5.
The Āryā consists of two types: the Pathyā and the Vipulā.
When the two odd-numbered feet are completed with three *ca* syllables [at their ends], then it is the Pathyā.
When even a single odd quarter-verse is not completed by three *ca* syllables, it is indeed *vipulā*.
Among these, the examples for *pathyā* are the preceding sūtras.
But this *sūtra* belongs to *Vipulā*. If the second and fourth *gaṇas*, called *ja*, are situated between heavy [syllables], they should occur in both halves; then it would be *Sarvacapalā*. (6)
If the second gaṇa is called *ja* (jagaṇa) and the fourth is likewise, and if two heavy syllables (*guru*) exist between them in both halves, then the Āryā is *sarvacapalā*.
However, if this characteristic of the *capalāpāda* exists only in the first half, [it is] *ardhacapalā*.
Furthermore, she does not become talkative during the latter half of the day. ||7||

The definition of *capalā* is as follows: if the second and fourth feet consist of *ja*, *u*, and two *gurus* situated in the middle, and this occurs only in the first half (*pūrvārdha*) and not in the second half (*aparārdha*), then it is *mukhacapalā*.
This is stated by excluding the previously mentioned definition of *capalā* from the first half.
That jaghanacapalā [meter] exists by depending on one [syllable] from the latter half. ||8||
In the Āryā meter, where the characteristic of *capalā* previously described applies to the latter half alone while omitting the former half, that is *jaghanacapalā*.
It is also [called *capalā*] when the sixth *gaṇa* in both halves consists of either a *ja* (*jagaṇa*) or a *kha* (*khagaṇa*).
And as with the first half, the remaining [half] has a fixed rule; that is *gīti*. ||9||
In the *āryā*, where the sixth *gaṇa* in both halves may be either *ja* or *kha*,
and the remaining rules regarding the placement of pauses (*yati*) and so forth are the same, while the second half is also like the first half— that is called *gīti*.
That [meter] in which the sixth gaṇa occurs on both halves, and the remainder follows the rule of the latter half, they call that Upagīti. (10)
They call that *upagīti* in which the sixth *gaṇa* is *ka* in both halves, and where the remaining rules regarding pauses and so forth in the first half are the same as in the second half; however,
in the first half the sixth may be *ka*, while in the latter half it is *ja* and *kha*.
The remaining specific arrangement arises from the reversal of the petals; thus there is the *saṅgīti*. ||11||
In this [meter], if the sixth *gaṇa* in the first half of the noble [verse] is *ka*,
and in the second half it is either *ja* or *kha*, the remaining rules regarding pauses (*yati*) and so forth may also vary according to the inversion of the two halves.
That which was made in the latter half occurs in the former half, and that which was made from the former half occurs in the latter half;
that is the *saṅgīti*. In each of its petals there are eight syllables, and the sixth *gaṇa* is either *ja* or *kha*.
And as in the case of the first half, the remaining [half] is subject to specific restriction; thus there is the *sāryāgīti*. ||12||
That Āryā in which there are eight gaṇas called *cagaṇa* (four short syllables) in each half,
while the sixth gaṇa is either a *jagaṇa* or a *khagaṇa*,
and the remaining rules regarding pauses (*yati*) and so forth are the same as in the first half of the Āryā— that is the Āryāgīti.
In the eighth [foot], there should be no *bhaja* or *kha* gaṇas, because of the requirement for a heavy syllable at the end of the half-verse. [These are] the Āryā-jātis.

When there are three *da* syllables at the beginning of the odd feet, and four *ya* syllables followed by *ra*, *la*, and *ga* in the even feet, it is called Vaitālīya; provided that in the even feet, six *la* syllables do not occur consecutively. (13)
The syllable *da* is said to consist of two morae (*dvimātra*).
There should be three *da*s at the beginning of the odd quarters and four *da*s at the beginning of the even quarters;
furthermore, there is a *ra* after both types of quarters.

If *la*s and *ga*s should occur, and if a sequence of six consecutive light syllables (*laghu*) does not appear in the even quarters (*pāda*), that is called *vaitālīya*. If it resembles *vaitālīya* at the beginning (*mukha*) but has *ra* and *ya* at the end (*pṛṣṭha*), it is *aupacchandasika*. (14)
If there is a *ra* and a *ya* at the end of the first half (the "back") equal to the *vaitālīya* in the first half (the "face"), that is *aupacchandasika*.
In this case, the *āpātalikā* has *bha*, *ga*, and *na* at the end; its face is identical to the *vaitālīya*. (15)
In its first half, there should be two *da*s, a *tri*, and a *catuṣka*; at the end, where *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* occur, that is *āpātalikā*.
In the second half, following the *da*s, there are *ja* and *da*; the *prācyavṛtti* is like the first [half], but with the *aśiṣṭa* [variation]. (16)

If the *jadau* (the syllables *ja* and *da*) occur at the beginning of the two even feet (*yugmapādayoḥ*), while the remaining characteristics are identical to those of *vaitālīya*, then it is *prācyavṛtti*.
*Udīcyavṛtti* occurs when the *jadau* are at the beginning of the odd feet (*mayujoḥ*), and the remainder is like the first [verse]. (17)
If there is *ja* and *da* at the beginning of the odd feet, while the remainder is identical to the *vaitālīya*, that is the *udīcyavṛtti*.
The *pravṛttaka* consists of the *udīcyavṛtti* in the odd feet and the *prācyavṛtti* in the even feet. (18)

That which consists of an odd pair of feet from the *udīcīvṛtta* and an even pair of feet from the *prācīvṛtta* is the *pravṛttaka*. When the *yati* (caesura) occurs at the end of the second foot, it is the *aparāntikā*. (19)
*Apārāntikā* consists of four feet with *pravṛttaka* and *yugmapāda*; *Cāruhāsinī* consists of odd-numbered feet. ||20||
Cāruhāsinī consists of the *pravṛttaka* meter with uneven four-footed lines.
[These are] the *vaitālīya* meters.
At every step on the shore, his firmness became unsteady and wavering.

"Padi-padi" means "at every foot"; thus, when there are four *ca* syllables (long syllables) in all the feet, it is *acaladhṛti*. At the end, it is *mātrāsamaka* because of the *li* syllable (the *la-gaṇa*). ||22||

If there are two half-cakāras (ca) in the *dala* of the feet, and if there are four cakāras in all the feet, with two light syllables (*laghu*) in the subsequent *dala* of the *gantā*, it is *mātrāsamaka*.
O friend, if there are two *ca*s from the *upacitrā*, [it is *mātrāsamaka*]. (23)
If there are four *ca*s in the quarters (*pādas*), and a *bha* follows two *ca*s, then it is *upacitrā*. Or, if after two *ca*s there is a *kha* or a *ja*, it is *viśloka*. (24)
If there are four *ca* syllables in the quarters (*pāda*), and after the *ca* there is either *kha* or *ja*, then it is *viśloka*.
Or, according to the half-verse of Vānavāsika, it is *kho* or *jo*. (25)
If there are four *ca* syllables in each quarter, and after the middle [of the first half] there is either *kha* or *ja*, then it is called *Vānavāsikā*.
If there is a pair of *sa*s, it is *Citrā*. (26)
If there are four *ca* syllables in each quarter (*pāda*), followed by a *ca* and then two *sa*s, that is *citrā*.
A *kulaka* consists of quarters beginning with *mātrāsamaka* and so forth, possessing the characteristics described immediately above.
The Sage has declared the *pādākulaka* meter, which encompasses an unknown number of syllabic instants (*vṛtta*) and morae (*mātrā*). ||27||

Taking at will those feet of the five types beginning with *mātrāsamaka* which have been specified by the definition just stated, Piṅgala has declared that when they are combined in a confused manner, that is the definition of *pādākulaka*.
This is because the measure of the verse (*vṛtta*) is fixed, and thus, through such a combination, all five varieties occur in their proper sequence.

That [meter] which has eight and eight syllables in each half-verse is called Anaṅgakrīḍā; the other [variety], however, consists entirely of six light syllables multiplied by the number of oceans (four), with the extension of feet arranged above. 28.

That [meter] in which there are sixteen heavy syllables (*guru*) in the first half of every quarter and thirty-two light syllables (*laghu*) placed in the second half is called *anaṅgakrīḍā*; it is exceedingly beautiful, with its heavy syllables arranged at the end of each ten-light-syllable segment in every petal. (29)
That meter in which there are four *ca* syllables in each quarter, and thirty light syllables followed by a heavy syllable in both halves, is called *atirucirā*.
It is defined as *cadakadakatricaṃ jagiti khaṇḍamajaṃ bharahitamanādime*. (30)
If in each quarter there are *ca*, *da*, *ka*, *da*, *ka*, three *ja*s, and *ga*, it would be a *khaṇḍa*;
this applies elsewhere than what has been stated where the letter *ja* does not occur.
Furthermore, that which exceeds the first group and is elsewhere devoid of the letter *bha*—
such as *cadaka-dakatri-caṃ jagiti*, *khaṇḍamajaṃ*, and *bhara-hita-mahādi-me*—
is the sixth chapter.
Although the meters (*vṛtta*) have already been mentioned previously, they were not presented in their entirety but rather according to their relative importance.
Since the totality of those meters is vast, the sixfold system beginning with the *prastāra* (the expansion chart) is now set forth for the sake of thorough understanding.

In the first [meter] of the Prastāra, all syllables are heavy; in the next, the syllable following the first heavy one is light, and the subsequent ones are similar to those preceding them. Continue this process until all syllables are light. ||1||
The Paiṅgala Prastāra.
In the procedure for constructing the *prastāra*, one should first write a meter consisting entirely of heavy syllables (*sarvaguru*).
Then, beneath the first heavy syllable, place a light syllable (*laghu*),
while the others remain identical.

The three types [of breaths], beginning with "the eastern cows," should be performed as appropriate. These too should be performed until the entire movement has become light. Among the heavy [breaths], that which is at the beginning is the eldest heavy [breath].
Below that, one should write "light" (laghu).
Then the subsequent [syllables] are like the first, with the preceding one being heavy (guru).
Thus is the Paiṅgala-prastāra.

In the *prastāra* (metrical grid), the *paṅkti* meter is doubled in length; each subsequent *praticchanda* increases successively by double the number of *gaṇas* consisting of heavy and light syllables. ||2||
This is our own arrangement.
In the process of constructing the *prastāra*, a heavy syllable (*guru*) should be written above and a light syllable (*laghu*) below;
thus, there arises a meter (*chandas*) of one syllable.

Having first performed the multiplication of the established [number] by its length for each meter, the preceding row increases successively by doubling the immediately following heavy and light syllables.
This is our *prastāra* (diagrammatic table).

To determine what the *vṛtta* (meter) at this specific position is, one should place [the numbers] and divide by the result; for an odd number, divide after adding one, and for an even number here, divide by two.
Thus, 'ga' results from the process, and 'la' results when the number is even. This is how the "lost" (*naṣṭa*) [meter] is determined. ||3||
When one desires to ask about a single uneven meter,
then this is the rule:
such a perfection would be of this extent.
For example, when it is asked how a *daśavṛtta* occurs within a meter of four syllables,
one should immediately write down ten and divide [the number] until the result is lost;
"division" (*dala*) means halving.

In that regard, wherever there is an uneven [number of syllables], one should place a single [long syllable] there, making it even, and then divide it; the meaning is that in an uneven division, a *guru* (heavy syllable) is obtained. However, the rule "in an even [division] there is a *la*" means that in an even division, a *laghu* (light syllable) is obtained.
Whatever [number] is obtained, one should write each of those individually across the line; thus what has arisen bears fruit, while what is lost is the "eye" (the zero). "Lost" refers to the eye.
One should write here, in order, the numbers one and so on, doubled, beneath the verse, noting which verse-number it is;
then, in that column of light-syllables with one added, the verse-number indicated is that manyth.

When it is known which position a *vṛtta* occupies by its own nature, yet it is not known what kind of *vṛtta* it is, the method for enumeration (*uddiṣṭividhi*) is applied for the sake of that knowledge. For example, when asked "Which *vṛtta* is this in a four-syllable meter with two heavy syllables in the middle?",
one should write the figure of that very *vṛtta* below a line and, above the line, write the numbers in sequence starting from one, each doubled in order, corresponding to the positions passed.
By this, that should be clearly stated:
there, whatever number is above the small [quantities], one should add one to that in the aggregate above the small [quantity].
By performing it in this manner, the number obtained should be understood as the indicated value "to this extent."
Here, there is one light syllable above and eight [others],
which together amount to nine;
with the addition of one more, they become ten.
By this, there would be the knowledge that "that event is the tenth.
This is the rule for the enumeration (*uddiṣṭividhi*).
Having placed the form (*rūpa*), one should rise by means of throws equal to the number of syllables (*akṣara*) above the even [position].
The *vṛtta* [meter] consists of heavy syllables (*gurubhiḥ*) and light syllables (*laghubhiḥ*), with the latter being either one or more than one, arranged in regular or irregular sequences. 5.
The Paiṅgalī Laghukriyā.

In this context of Vedic prosody (*chandas*), when one wishes to know how many meters (*vṛtta*) have no short syllables (*alaghu*), how many have only one short syllable, how many have two short syllables, and so forth, then the procedure for determining short syllables (*laghukriyā*) is applied.
"Form" (rūpa) has a single meaning; in that regard, having first placed one [unit] below, one should rise up from there in sequence,
with each letter proceeding in equal number, level by level, directly above its own respective base.
For example, in a meter of four syllables, there are four [syllables];

by this, there would be five [combinations] for each. Among those, there is one arising from a single [syllable] and one from four [syllables]. In sequence, within the intervals of the light-syllable combinations, there is one arising from three [syllables].
In two places and one place, and so on until the completion of the task; one, two, three, and so forth, up to that limit, one should write them on the side.
If it is asked, "What would be the accomplishment? [the answer is:
one [foot] with no light syllables, and one with four light syllables.
There are six with two short syllables,
four with three short syllables, and one consisting entirely of short syllables.

In this way, the treatment of light syllables (*laghukriyā*) is the same as that of heavy syllables (*gurukriyā*); therefore, even a meter such as *aguru-ekaguru* (one light and one heavy) should be understood accordingly.
Thus ends the *paiṅgalī laghukriyā*.
Having set aside the first form even if it has no [corresponding] number, one should then write [the numbers] below;
by mixing each with its own respective lower [number], there arise the vṛtta types such as aladhva, ekaladhva, and so forth.
This is our brief procedure.
First, one should draw the form.
Regarding the phrase "even when not performed, it is a light task," this refers to the meter consisting of the single syllable *e*.
By the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that it is so even when [the rite] has been performed.
Then, having set aside that initial form and placed it aside, one should write the number of syllables of the meter in its place.

For example: in the case of a one-syllable meter or a two-syllable meter, having set aside that same initial form, one should write the number in its place. Having likewise written the number for the three-syllable meter, one should then take the "two" situated below that and combine it with the one directly beneath it.
In the same way, one should write the number for four syllables;
then, one should mix the three situated below with the single unit of each respective lower triad.
This is our "Easy Method" (laghukriyā).

What is the number of syllables in the meters? The squares [of the number of syllables] multiplied by the number of Yamas (two) is the form. In the case of *uddiṣṭa*, the last [value] is doubled, and there is also a sum for the operation of light syllables (*laghu*). ||7||
When the inquiry "How many meters (*vṛtta*) are there in this *chandas*? arises, there are three methods. For example: having set down the form for four syllables, one should double it four times;
or else, according to the method of *uddiṣṭa*, the numbers are one, two, [three, etc.]...
Four and eight;
at their end, one should make the eight doubled.
Alternatively, it is the *laghukriyā*.
One,
four, six, and one with four— these are to be combined among them.
By this, the meters (*vṛtta*) would be sixteenfold;
such is the number of meters. That very number multiplied by the syllables (*varṇa*), then its half, and then the sum of both [halves].
First are the heavy syllables among the phonemes, followed by the light ones; after that come the morae. ||8||

In this context, by the word *varṇa*, vowels that are not fixed among the consonants are called *akṣaras*. This rule applies when one desires to know the number of syllables in a meter (*vṛtta*). For example: if the number of syllables in a four-syllable meter is sixteen, this very number written at the beginning is to be multiplied by the four syllables.
Beyond that, half of that [is the next], and beyond that as well, both together form a *piṇḍa*.

There are sixty-four syllables (*akṣara*), thirty-two heavy and light syllables (*guru-laghu*), and ninety-six morae (*mātrā*). Among these, first there are sixty-four syllables; in the middle, there are also thirty-two heavy and light syllables.
But first, there are ninety-six measures;
this is the count of syllables, heavy syllables, light syllables, and measures.
The horizontal and downward paths consist of twice the number of phonemes minus one.
For the ground of those that are heavy and light, as well as of those in between, is indeed equal. ||9||
In this regard, when there is a desire to know how large the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) of the meters is, and how far it extends horizontally and vertically, this is the rule: for example,
in the case of a four-syllable meter, that four-syllable [unit] doubled and multiplied by seven less one would result [in the total].
Therefore, even a barley-corn or a finger-breadth is a transverse path.
Those sixteen circles, when doubled, would be twenty-nine.
Hence, a barley-corn, a finger-breadth, and so forth, is a downward path of thirty-one [units].
In this manner, as many heavy units (gurubhūmi) as there are, so many light units (laghubhūmi) should be conceived.
As many lines as there are, so many [units] are there in their intervals.
Thus, in due order, there is the expansion (prastāra), as well as the methods for the lost (naṣṭa) and the indicated (uddiṣṭa) meters.
Number, as well as connection with time, and the six suffixes in verses—these are the [topics]. (10)
The six [types of] meters beginning with *prastāra* are indicators for even (*samavṛtta*) meters,
not for half-even (*ardhasama*) or uneven (*viṣama*) meters.
Nor [do they arise] from births,
because that is illogical.
If it is asked, "How then do those conditions [arise]?"
Thus, since a condition is not perceived through its mere slight distinction,
even the superior knowledge of the authors of treatises is correctly perceived, just as it is by astronomers regarding the movement of Rāhu and other such phenomena in the science of astrology.
In all the *prastāras* of even meters (*samavṛtta*), six principles have been stated.
Now, the knowledge of the number of heavy and light syllables and morae (*mātrā*) in each individual meter (*vṛtta*) or class of meters (*jāti*) is being set forth.
Here are two verses as examples.

Victorious are those—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—who are the supreme ultimate reality, who abide on the path that leads to the fruit of all ultimate goals, and who are the persons produced thereby. || 1 ||
Victorious is the Jina, whose essence is the Dharma; victorious is his companion, Prajñā;
and victorious is the assembly of noble ones, whose bodies are the fruit of the seeds of liberation such as Upāya.
In this [meter], there are fifty-seven mātrās,
forty syllables,
and seventeen heavy syllables.
There are twenty-three *laghus*.

Having shown these two numbers, because the others become clear according to their application, they should be observed at the end of the process of placement (*nyāsakarman*) both below and above the *mātrās*.
The *mātrās* of those [syllables] devoid of *laghus* are half of the *mātrās* when the syllables are excluded from the *laghus*.
And just as the morae are devoid of color, so too are there that many heavy syllables here.
When asked: "There are 40 syllables (varṇas) and 57 morae (mātrās); there are 23 short syllables (laghus). How many long syllables (gurus) are there? [the answer is as follows:]
They should be joined at the beginning and the end;
having placed them in the middle, they should be split.
By this, there will be seventeen *gurus*.
The number of gurus.

The quantity of syllables is twice as many as the number of heavy syllables; likewise, the number of light syllables here is exactly equal to the number of syllables minus the number of heavy syllables. (12)
Mātrās: 57, syllables (varṇas): 40, heavy syllables (gurus): 17; mātrās: 57, heavy syllables: 17. Having doubled the heavy syllables at the beginning, one should calculate the mātrās.
Having doubled the syllables (varṇas) in the middle, one should join them with the prosodic measures (mātrās); at the end, one should join the heavy syllables (gurus).
By this means, there will be twenty-three light syllables (laghus).
The small number.

As many as are the sums of heavy and light syllables, as many as are the morae excluding the heavy syllables, and as many as are half the sum of the light syllables—so many are the syllables here. 13.

Seventeen heavy syllables (gurus), fifty-seven morae (mātrās), fifty-seven morae, twenty-three light syllables (laghus), seventeen heavy syllables, and twenty-three light syllables are to be placed at the beginning.
It should be joined in the middle and split at the end;
by this, there are forty syllables.
The enumeration of the phonemes.
The number of syllables, when doubled and diminished by the light syllables, and likewise the number of syllables mixed with heavy ones, are here equal to the number of morae (mātrās). 14.
There are 23 light syllables, 40 letters, 40 letters, 17 heavy syllables, 23 light syllables, and 17 heavy syllables; first, the heavy syllables should be placed by doubling them.
In the middle, the syllables should be doubled; the short syllables should be joined; at the end, they should be mixed.
By this, there would be fifty-seven mātrās;
such is the count of mātrās.
Whatever merit has been born from my propitiating this knowledge of the Jina, may the world propitiate that supreme knowledge through the ultimate truths. (15)
(Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Chandoratnākara* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
The work titled *Chandoratnākara*, the composition of the venerable Ratnākaraśānti, the omniscient one of the Kali age, is completed.
May there be auspiciousness for all the world!
This work is the composition of the venerable Śāntipāda, the ocean of jewels and the omniscient one of the Kali age.
It was written by the Śākya bhikṣu Dharmapālabhadra, the foremost jewel among the eyes of the world.
Furthermore, it was spoken by Jaṅchupacemo (Bodhiśekhara), the incomparable great lord of the three worlds, whose names are proclaimed [as such].

Furthermore, based on the explanatory notes on the verses and relying upon the permission granted by that very master— who was protected by compassion for virtuous beings— the illustrious Bhikṣu Nam-mkha’-bsam-pa (Ratnadharmapālabhadra) revised [this work].
May he, too, benefit all sentient beings through this jewel of the Buddha’s teaching.
The *Chandoratnākara*, a work by the venerable Śānti, the omniscient jewel-mine of the Kali age, is hereby completed.
This was translated by the virtuous Rasavāyaraluṅgapā Ṅagpā Gyalachena (Kīrtidhvaja).
Furthermore, it was [revised] for the sake of the incomparable Great Omniscient One of the Three Worlds, by Jaṅchupacemo (Bodhiśekhara), who is designated by his spoken name.

Furthermore, based on the words of that very teacher and relying upon his permission to speak, the Śākya bhikṣu Nam mkha’ bzang po (Ākāśabhadra)— who was protected by the compassion of that noble master, who was adorned with the crest-jewel of supreme restraint and diligence, and who was a peerless sovereign among the masters of the Tripitaka and the two types of linguistic analysis— translated, extracted, and edited this work from the manuscript of the illustrious Lo ston Dpal gyi mgon po (Śrīmān Sthiramati), having transcribed it from the Indian script into the Tibetan script at the great monastic center of Śrī E vam.
The third chapter:
among even meters (*samavṛtta*), there is one characteristic for all four quarters;
among half-even meters (*ardhasama*), there is another for the two even quarters.
And there is another [type] for the odd [feet].
The first and third feet are odd;
the second and fourth feet are even.
*Yugma*, *yugya*, and *sama* are synonyms;
*ayugma*, *ayuja*, and *viṣama* are synonyms. They call the *upacitraka* that which has odd-numbered *yatis*.
If there are thirty-one *laghu*s and then three *guru*s, [it is the Vaitālīya meter]. ||1||
If in the odd feet (the first and third), there should be *sa*,
*sa*, a short syllable (*laghu*), and a long syllable (*guru*);
And when there are three *bha* gaṇas in both even feet, followed by two *ga*s,
then they call that the *upacitraka* metre. (For example— )

In the case of half-equal meters, because they consist of half-measures, the verse should be constructed by repeating [the pattern] twice. If there are three *bha*s followed by a *ga*, it is *Drutamadhyā*; if, however, there are *na*, *ja*, and two *ja*s, it is likewise [the same]. (2)
If in the odd feet there are two *gurus* after three *bhas*,
and if in the even feet there are *na*, *ja*, *ja*, and *ya*, [then it is the Vaitālīya meter].
If it has three *s* (short) syllables followed by a *guru* (long), it is *drutamadhyā*;
if it has three *bhagaṇas* (— ◡◡) followed by a *ga* (short), it is *vegavatī*.

If there are three *sa*s (short syllables) followed by a long syllable (*guru*) in the odd feet, and if after the third *bha* (the syllables *ta-ta-ga*) there are two long syllables (*guru*) in the even feet, then it is *vegavatī*.
In that [meter], the odd [pādas] consist of ta, ja, ra, pha, and ga; the even [pādas] consist of ma, sa, ja, ga, and ga; this is the Bhadravirāj. ||4||
In which [meter], there are *ta*, *ja*, *ra*,
and *ga* in the odd quarters, and *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga* in the even quarters.
And when there are [six] ga-gaṇas,
that is Bhadravirāj; if it is uneven, it is Sama if it consists of sa, ja, sa, and ga.
In the *ketuvata* [meter], there are *bha*, *ra*, *pha*, *na*, *ga*, and *ga*. ||5||
If there are *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *ga* in the odd feet (*ayugmapāda*),
and *bha*, *ra*, [and *na*] in the even feet (*yugmapāda*), [it is the *vaitālīya* meter].
If the [syllables] na, guru,
and ga occur, it is *ketuvatī*; it would be *ākhyānikā* if those two [jagatī feet] were followed by ga.
But *stvyuk* is the name of the *jagatī* meter when it consists of *ja*, *ta*, *ga*, and *ga*. ||6||

If in the odd feet (the first and third) there are *ja*, *ta*, *ja*, and a heavy syllable (*g*), and in the even feet (the second and fourth) there are *ja*, *ta*, [and a heavy syllable], [it is the Vaitālīya meter].
When there are *ja*, *ga*, and *guru* [syllables], then it is the *ākhyānikā*.
If those two [ga-ga] are followed by ja, ga, and ā, it would be the Ākhyānikā; this Ākhyānikā is the reverse of the previous one.
Wherein, in the odd pādas, there should be ja, ta, ja, ga, and ga;
If, however, in both even feet, those two (ja and ga) along with a long syllable (guru) occur, that is called Ākhyānikā with the [other] preceding [meter] reversed.
If there are three *sat* gaṇas followed by a *la* and a *ga*, and then *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *sa*, then it is the *hariṇaplutā* metre. (8)
If in the odd feet there is *sa*, *tri*, and after them a short (*la*) and a long (*ga*), and in the even feet *na*,
*bha*, *bha*, [it is the *Vaitālīya*].
If there are *ra*, *sa*, and *yu*,
then it is the *hariṇaplutā*.
If there are *na*, *na*, *ra*, *la*, *ga*, *na*, *ja*, and *ja* followed by *ra*, [then it is the *hariṇaplutā*].
And if, at that time, it is intended as an aparavaktra [meter], ||9||
If in the odd quarters there are *na*, *na*, *ra*, a light syllable (*laghu*), and a heavy syllable (*guru*), and in the even quarters there are *na*...
When there are *ja*, *ja*, and *ra*, it is then desired as *aparavaktra*.
If there is *ya*, *yu*, *ga*, *i*, *ha*, and if there is a pair of *na*, *ra*, *ya*, *ya*, followed by *ja*, *ja*, *ra*, *ga*, they call it *puṣpitāgra*. (10)
The word *iha* refers to those meters with equal halves. If, in the odd feet, there should be *na*, *na*, *ra*, and *ya*, [then it is the Vaitālīya].
And in our even feet, there are *ja*,
*ja*, *ra*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*).
Then they call it *puṣpitāgrā*.
These two are varieties of *vaitālīya*:
*repha-ja-ra-ja*, as well as *ja-ra-ja* and *ja-ra-ga*.
The suffix *matup* is used in the feminine gender when it expresses the same meaning as the word [ending in the feminine suffix] *ī*.
If there are two *ra*s in the odd feet,
and *ja*, *ra*, *ja*, *ra* in the even feet;
If they should be heavy, then it is "yavamatī.
Since the suffix *matup* exists in the word "yava," it signifies that very thing; thus, by designating the feminine form, the meaning is "yavamatī" (possessing barley).

If the odd [pādas] consist of ten, ten, and two short syllables, and the other [even pādas] likewise consist of ten, ten, and ten short syllables, with a long syllable at the end—provided that both have a gracefully extended arrangement of feet—it is the Śikhā metre. (12)
If there are twenty-eight light syllables in the odd feet and thirty light syllables in the even feet,
and if both [feet] end with a heavy syllable, it is *lalitapadavisṛti*.
Then it becomes the *aśikhā*.

With its petals arranged by the exchange of its own abodes as expressed through even and uneven feet, this [meter] here in the world invariably receives the name "Kuṭilapadanigaḍana" (The Shackles of Crooked Feet). 13.
That place which is described as being fixed by both even and uneven [feet] is devoid of restriction;
where the arrangement of half-verses is reversed, this is known here in the world as *nigaḍita* (the fettered).
A verse with crooked feet, however, is known as *nigaḍita*.
Likewise, for that whose designation is a corresponding name, the meaning is that it is "bound" in this manner.
[This concludes] the Half-Same Meters (*ardhasamavṛtta*).
The Fourth Chapter:
That meter in which there is no equality of heavy and light syllables, or equality of phonemes (varṇa), across all four feet is called *viṣama* (irregular).
It is of four types: *vaktra*, *caturūrdhva*, *udgatā*, and *pracupita*.
In verses consisting of eight syllables per quarter, one should not take *sn* as the first two syllables if they are followed by *ya* and *ambu-dhi-vaktra*.
Excluding the first and the last, there is the *vaktra* variety of the *prastāra* known as "the middle of two groups.
If the quarters (*pāda*) consist of eight syllables,
then even there, provided there is no *sn* after the first syllable, if a *ya* follows the fourth [syllable], it is *vaktra*.
The first half-verse is indeed the preceding sūtra;
therefore, by repeating it twice, the verse is to be completed. When there is the letter *ja* in the even quarters, it is celebrated as the *vaktra* metre. (2)
The "face" (vaktra) is said to be the pathyā;
what then is its specific distinction?
It is that in the even quarters, after the ocean [the letter *m*], there is the letter *ja*.
This [type of *vipulā*] has been described as occurring at the end of the even (*yugma*) feet; it does not occur here at the beginning of the odd feet.
That which is wholesome (*pathyā*) becomes "unwholesome" (*viparītapathyā*) when it is reversed; this is the meaning. Here, the "mouth" (*vaktra*) is cited as an example of the *viparītapathyā*.
What is the distinction?
In the odd pādas, after the syllable *ja*, there is the ocean (four mātrās);
that same [rhythm] is known as Capalā when it occurs in the even pādas with the syllable *na*. (4)
That same [opening] is to be known as Capalā.
If one asks, "What is the distinction?
it is that after the fourth syllable (ambudhi) of the uneven feet, there is a *na* (nagaṇa).
That [verse] in which the seventh and the pair [of feet] are light is considered by the Sage to be the Vipulā. ||5||
That very same *vaktra* meter, in which the seventh syllable of both feet is light, is considered *vipulā* by the sage Piṅgala;
it remains that same [meter] for him in all respects.
In this metre, wherever—in every foot—the seventh syllable is light, that very [metre] is considered by that teacher to be Vipulā.
Beyond this, the verse should be composed by repeating [the rule] four times.
By means of the letter *bha*, from the ocean [of syllables], there is that Vipulā. (7)
The meaning is that when the subsequent *bha* occurs after the syllable *va*, they are "vimalā" (pure);
and by means of the letter *ra*, they are likewise [designated] as "vipulā" (expansive) from that point onward. ||8||
In every instance of the *vaktra* meter, after the syllable *ra*, there should be another [syllable] different from it;
thus, that *vipulā* is a *rakāravipulā* (or *ravipulā*). It is likewise with the syllable *na*. (9)

When there is a *para* [laghu] syllable at every position in the *vaktra* meter, it is called *vipulā*; when that same pattern occurs with a *na*-syllable [heavy syllable], it is *nakāra-vipulā* (also known as *navipulā*).
Likewise, it may also occur with a *ta*-syllable. ||10||
