When the syllable *ta* occurs everywhere in the opening (*vaktra*) of the ocean [meter], it is called *vipulā*; specifically, when it is *ta*, it is *takāra-vipulā* (or *tavipulā*).
It is likewise seen with the syllable *ma*. (11)
If that *vipulā* occurs everywhere in the opening (*vaktra*) with the syllable *ma*, even beyond the ocean (*ambudhi*), it is seen as *makāravipulā*;
for anything other than this is *vitāna*. ||12||
Whatever other characteristic of the *vaktra* meter exists beyond those characteristics already cited,
all of that is indeed the *vitāna*.
[In the *vitāna*,] there are *sa* and *na* at the beginning of every foot, and *ja* and *mbu* (ma-bha) in the even feet.
"In the case of uneven [feet], it should be as beautiful as possible"—this is generally observed in practice. (13)
Regarding those varieties of Vaktra that have been described, poets should generally observe similar applications in their compositions in brief:
thus, in all quarters (pādas), the syllables *sa* and *na* do not occur after the initial syllable;
and in the odd-numbered quarters, the syllable *ja* may occur after the syllable *ambu* (the fourth).
In the odd feet, after the syllable *ambudhi* (four), there should be *bha*, *ra*, *na*, *ta*, or *ma*; the remaining [syllables] are as desired for aesthetic beauty.
The Different Types of Faces.
The first foot consists of eight syllables,
and the subsequent ones increase by four each from that; that which possesses this, shining with various arrangements, is [the Vaitālīya].
The wise declare that the *padacaturūrdhva* meter possesses a path of gracefully modulated words. ||14||

The wise declare that when there are eight syllables in its first quarter, and each subsequent quarter increases by four syllables respectively, this uneven meter (*viṣamavṛtta*), which shines with various arrangements and possesses a charming path of words, is called *caturūrdhva*.
Its feet, moreover, should be understood according to their [respective] class and function from the group of limbs.
For example: the first foot is like the *padavaktra* foot in the Sūtra itself; the second is like the second foot of the Āryā; and the third and fourth are like the second half-verse of the Āryā.
In the *padacaturūrdhva* meter, there is a *prastāra* consisting of four [syllables per line];
the first [line] here in the *padacaturūrdhva* consists of eight syllables.

If all the light syllables are in the *gaganidhana* [meter], it brings joy to the world; however, when joined with the prefix *āṅ* and provided with a graceful pause (*yati*), it then becomes the *pīḍa* [meter].
In this context, within the *padacaturūrdhva* class itself, that [meter] in which there are two heavy syllables (*guru*) at the end of each quarter and all others are light,
and wherein the movement of the pause (*yati*) is gracefully applied, brings forth joy because it is of such a nature among the *jagatī* meters;
furthermore, when joined with the prefix *ā*, it becomes *pīḍa*.
The meaning is that even then it remains unafflicted.
If the first foot here steps near [the end of the second],
then the [second] foot [is considered short].
When the *parikṛta* (the first foot) has its residence in another [foot], while the other three remain in their own fixed positions, it is the *kalikā* metre. ||16||
In this case, if the first quarter-verse remains as an *āpīḍa* and, having passed over the second quarter-verse, does not further exceed the limit of the next [third] quarter-verse,
but rather dwells in the middle itself,
then the other three quarters dwell in their own respective abodes.
Such indeed would be the *kalikā* meter,
if the pair of feet were very close together and the first foot here were to fall into equality [with the others].
The triad of the other feet remains in its own unshakable abode; such is the graceful play of the *lava* meter. 17.
The first foot is indeed that of the *āpīḍa* meter; if it exceeds the second foot by three [syllables], while the other two feet remain exactly as they are, then it becomes *lavalīlā*.
The other three feet remain entirely unchanged.
If the first foot here falls into a *sam* [syllable count],
it is certainly a stream of nectar (*amṛtadhārā*), producing delight through its various prescribed and graceful pauses (*yati*). 18.

If the first foot of an *āpīḍa* consists of three feet situated within its own dwelling (the *vasantatilakā*) and it likewise produces delight through well-arranged graceful pauses (*yati*), then it certainly becomes a stream of nectar.
The Subdivisions of Padacaturūrdhva.
If first there are *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, and *la*s,

followed immediately by *na*, *sa*, *ja*, *ga*, and a heavy syllable (*guru*), and then, after two short syllables (*atha-ū*), there are *bha*, *na*, *ja*, *la*, and *ga*s; [then it is the Vamśastha meter].
And this [meter] is called Udgatā when it consists of sa, ja, sa, and ja. ||19||
If, in the first quarter, there are *ja*, *sa*, *sa*, and *laghu*;
immediately after that, in the second, *na*, *sa*, *ja*, and *guru*;
and then, in the third, *bha*, *na*, *ja*, *la*, and *ga*— [then it is the Vamśasthavila meter].
Furthermore, in the fourth [foot], there should be *sa*, *ja*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ga*; thus this is the *udgatā* meter. Indeed, three [feet] are exactly like the *udgatā*, while the third is otherwise.
It is known that this fragrance, composed of the letters *ra* and *na*, they describe as being of such a nature. ||20||

In this [meter], while the three feet other than the third are identical to the *udgatā*, the third foot is to be known as different. How so? "The third [foot] is otherwise, bound by *ra*, *na*, *bha*, and two heavy syllables (*guru*)."
When there is a triad of these two [gaṇas] followed by a *sayagaṇa* in the third foot,
it is the *lalita*, characterized by its gracefully extended arrangement of words.
For that which is called *lalita* (the graceful) is indeed desired by poets. ||21||
Where the third quarter consists of *na*, *u*, and *sa*, and the remaining quarters are similar to those of the *udgatā* meter,
that is indeed desired by poets as *lalita*.
Because it is charming through its extended arrangement of words,
[it is classified among] the varieties of *udgatā*.

If in the first quarter there are *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, *bha*, and two *gurus*, and then *sa*, *na*, *ja*, *ra*, *ga*, and further *na*, *sa*, [then it is the Vamśasthavila]; and if then *na*, *yu*, *ta*, *na*, *na*, *ja*, *ya*, [it is the Indravajrā].
This *pracupita* meter is declared to have been previously established. ||22||
If in the first quarter there should be *ma*, *sa*, *ja*, *bha*, and two heavy syllables (*guru*),
then in the second there should be *sa*, *na*, *ja*, *ra*, and a heavy syllable; and in the third, "furthermore" (*param*), there should be *na*, *na*, and *sa*.
Now, "atha" refers to the fourth [chapter], which has three [sections].
When *ja*, *ya*, and this [same sequence] occur together in one place, it becomes *Upasthitapracupita*.
If in a quarter there are *na*, *u*, *sa*, *na*, *na*, and *sa* in the third [foot], [it is *Upasthitapracupita*].
Poets call that the Vardhamāna;
here, another [meter] exists which is similar to the Pracupita, possessing the entire arrangement of characteristics for each fixed quarter-verse. 23.
If in the third foot there should be *na*, *na*, *sa*, *na*, *na*, and *sa*, and if here too the rule for all other feet is specified as being similar to that of the *Pracupita*,
then poets call it *Vardhamāna*.
When there are ta, ja, ra, and pha in this [meter], with a pause at the third [syllable] and the first, they call it Ārṣabha;
that is a specific variety of Śuddhavirāṭ.
If there is a subsequent triad of gaṇas equal to the *pracupita* [meter], [it is called *vaitālīya*]. ||24||
When the third foot consists of *ta*, *ja*, and *ra*, and there is a pause (*yati*) after its first syllable;
If its third foot were identical to the *pracupita* gaṇa, then that specific variety of *śuddhavirāj* is called by the name *ārṣabha*; they call that metrical pattern *śuddhavirāḍārṣabha*.
These are the subdivisions of *pracupita*.
The Fifth Chapter. The varieties of *vṛtta* have been explained; from here onwards, the *jāti*s must be described.
A single *mātrā* does not consist of a consonant alone; it consists of one light (*laghu*) syllable or two heavy (*guru*) syllables.
The varieties of *vṛtti* have been stated; now the *jāti*s must be explained. *Jāti* is also of three kinds: *āryā*,...
The *vaitālīya* and the *mātrāsamaka*.

Among these, the *āryā* resembles the uneven meters (*viṣamavṛtta*) in having more than three syllables [in its first half], while the *vaitālīya* resembles the half-even meters (*ardhasamavṛtta*) in having more than two [syllable-groups] in the latter part.

The *mātrāsamaka* meter, which is distinct from the three [types] of *ūrdhva*, resembles the *samavṛtta* class; in this meter as well, the calculation is by *mātrās* and not by consonants (*vyañjana*). However, one short syllable (*laghu*) constitutes one *mātrā*.
With one *guru* there are two *mātrās*.
Five *bhajasas*, a pair of *gurūs*, and four *laghus* constitute *gaṇas* of four *mātrās*.
Among them, *ca* and *kha* consist of four *laghus*; *ka* consists of one *mātrā*; and *da* consists of two *mātrās*. (2)
Among the groups of four morae, there are the *bha* group, the *ja* group, and the *sa* group.
There are two *gurus* and four *laghus*, making five;
these five groups (*gaṇas*) are also designated by the name *casa*. Among these groups, the fifth consists of four *laghus*.
That [syllable] is designated as *kha* and also as *ca*;
however, a *gaṇa* consisting of a single *mātrā* is designated as *ka*.
But that which consists of two mātrās is called *da*.
It too is of two kinds: either two short syllables (*laghu*) or a single long syllable (*guru*).
If, in the odd [feet], it is devoid of *ja* and *ra*, there are eight *gaṇas* in each half; this is the *Āryā*.
In the latter half, the sixth is *ka*, the eighth is *da*, and in both [halves] the remaining syllables are *ca*. ||3||
If there are eight *gaṇas* in both halves [of the verse], then it is an *āryā*.
How are there eight?
By the omission of the letter *ja* in the odd positions—namely, the first, third, fifth, and seventh.
In that regard, having combined the sixth gaṇa into a single mātrā in the latter half, there are two mātrās in the eighth gaṇa of both halves, while the remaining [gaṇas] consist of four mātrās each;
furthermore, the eighth [syllable] is never short (laghu).
Because of the heaviness at the end of the half-verse:
in the first half, the sixth syllable is either *ja* or *kha*, provided there is no light syllable following the *kha*;
the pause (*yati*) occurs after the sixth syllable, or if followed by a *kha*, it occurs at the end; furthermore, in the latter half, the fourth syllable also becomes the pause.
In the first half [of the verse], the sixth *gaṇa* should be made as the letter *ja*, as in the previous rule;
or else, as in this rule, it should be the letter *kha*.
When the sixth [syllable] of the first half would be *kha*, [it is so].
In that case, however, the pause (yati) must be made at the first short syllable, provided that the sixth gaṇa in the first half-verse is followed by a "kha" (i.e., a long syllable);
for "khapara" means that which has a "kha" following it.
Then it is the sixth;
at its end, a pause (yati) should be made.
That which has a pause at the end is called "antayati."
If, in the last leaf (pada), in its latter half, the fourth gaṇa should be "khapara" (consisting of a short syllable followed by two long syllables),
or— by virtue of the word "api"— even the sixth [gaṇa] should be so,
then a pause (yati) must also be made at the end.
Therefore, the group of one mātrā is beautiful.
In one place, because of the word "ending in the nominative case" (*prathamāntavat*), it consists of that which ends in [the nominative].
For this very reason, in the first half, the sixth [letter] is indeed *kha*.
The pause occurs at the beginning of the sixth [syllable].
In the seventh [syllable], which is indeed *kha*, when followed by a sixth [syllable], there is a pause;
in the latter half, the fifth [syllable] is indeed *kha*.
The seventh syllable is indeed a pause (yati) after the fourth [syllable], and there is a pause after the sixth; this is the definition for all pauses. The example, however, is the sūtra itself.
When both odd-numbered feet are completed by those three [syllables], then it is *pathyā*;
if even one of them is not concluded by those odd-numbered feet, then it is *vipulā*. 5.
The Āryā is of two kinds: Pathyā and Vipulā.
When the two odd-numbered feet are completed with three *ca* syllables [at their ends], then it is Pathyā.
When not even a single odd foot is completed with three *ca* syllables,
then it is indeed *vipulā*. Regarding that, the previous sūtras provide examples of *pathyā*.
But this [verse] belongs to Vipulā.
If the second and fourth gaṇas, which are called *ja*, are situated between two heavy syllables (*guru*), and if they occur in both halves [of the verse], then it would be *Sarvacapalā*. (6)
If the second gaṇa is the one called *ja* (jagaṇa) and the fourth is likewise, and if two heavy syllables (*guru*) are present between them in both halves, then the Āryā is *sarvacapalā*.
However, if this characteristic of the *capalāpāda* occurs in the first half alone, it is simply *capalā*.
Furthermore, she does not become talkative during the latter half of the day. ||7||

The definition of *capalā* is as follows: if the second and fourth gaṇas are *ja*, and there are two heavy syllables (*guru*) situated in the middle, and this occurs only in the first half [of the verse] but not in the second half, then it is *mukhacapalā*.
This is stated by excluding the previously mentioned definition of *capalā* from the first half.
That *jaghanacapalā* [meter] exists by depending on a single [syllable] from the latter half [of the second line]. 8.
In the *āryā* meter, where the latter half alone— omitting the first half— possesses the characteristics of *capalā* as previously described, that is *jaghanacapalā*.
It occurs when the sixth *gaṇa* in both halves consists of either a *ja* (*jagaṇa*) or a *kha* (*khagaṇa*).
And like the first half, the remainder is fixed; that is *gīti*. ||9||
In the *āryā* meter, where the sixth *gaṇa* in both halves may be either *ja* or *kha*,
and the remaining rules regarding the placement of pauses (*yati*) and other constraints are identical, while the second half also follows the first half, that is called *gīti*.
That [meter] in which a *ṣaṣṭhagaṇa* occurs on both halves, and the remainder is like that of the *aparārdha*, they call it *upagīti*. 10.
They call that *upagīti* in which the sixth *gaṇa* is *ka* in both halves, and where the remaining rules regarding pauses and so forth are the same as in the first half for the second half as well;
however, where the sixth [gaṇa] in the first half is *ka*, but *ja* and *kha* (*jakhau*) occur in the latter half.
The remaining specific arrangement arises from the reversal of the petals; thus there is the *saṅgīti*. ||11||
In this [meter], if in the first half of the Āryā the sixth gaṇa is *ka*,
and in the second half it is either *ja* or *kha*, the remaining rules regarding pauses (*yati*) and so forth may also vary according to the inversion of the two halves.
That which was made in the latter half occurs in the former half, and that which was made from the former half occurs in the latter half;
that is the *saṅgīti*. In each of its petals there are eight syllables, and the sixth *gaṇa* is either *ja* or *kha*.
And as with the first half, the remainder is subject to specific restriction; thus there is the *sāryāgīti*. ||12||
That Āryā in which there are eight *gaṇas* called *cagaṇas* (four short syllables) in each half,

while the sixth *gaṇa* may be either a *ja-gaṇa* or a *kha-gaṇa*, and the remaining rules regarding pauses (*yati*) and so forth are the same as those for the first half of the *Āryā*, is the *Āryāgīti*.
In the eighth [foot], there should not be *bhaga*, *ja*, or *kha* [gaṇas], because of the heaviness at the end of the half-verse. [These are] the Āryā-jātis.

When there is a group of three at the beginning of the odd feet, and a group of four in the even feet, with *ra*, *la*, and *ga* following thereafter, it is called Vaitālīya; provided that in the even feet, six short syllables do not occur consecutively. (13)
The syllable *da* is said to have two morae (*dvimātra*).
There should be three *da*s at the beginning of the odd quarters and four *da*s at the beginning of the even quarters;
furthermore, there should be a *ra* after both types of quarters.

If *la*s and *ga*s should occur, and if a sequence of six consecutive light syllables (*laghu*) does not exist in the two even quarters (*pāda*), that is called *vaitālīya*. If it resembles *vaitālīya* at the beginning (*mukha*) but has *ra* and *ya* at the end (*pṛṣṭha*), it is *aupacchandasika*. (14)
If there is a *ra* and a *ya* at the end of the first half, equal to the *vaitālīya*, and likewise at the end of the second half, that is the *aupacchandasika*.
Here, the first half of the *āpātalikā* is identical to the *vaitālīya*, ending with the *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* gaṇas. (15)
In its first half, there should be three *da*s and a *catuṣka* (four *ga*s), and at the end, where *bha*, *ga*, and *ga* occur, it is *āpātalikā*.
In the pair of halves, if *ja* and *da* follow two *da*s, it is *prācyavṛtti*; otherwise, it is *aśiṣṭā*, being like the first [type]. (16)

If the *jadau* (the syllables *ja* and *da*) occur at the beginning of the two even feet (*yugmapāda*), and the remaining characteristics are identical to those of *vaitālīya*, then it is *prācyavṛtti*.
When the *jadau* occur at the beginning of the two odd feet (*ayujaḥ*), and the remainder is like the first [verse], it is *udīcyavṛtti*. (17)
If there is a *ja* and a *da* at the beginning of the odd feet, and the remainder is the same as in *vaitālīya*, that is *udīcyavṛtti*.
The *udīcyavṛtti* possesses the odd feet [of *vaitālīya*], while the *prācyavṛtti* possesses the even feet; this is *pravṛttaka*. (18)

That which consists of an odd-numbered pair of feet based on the Udīcya-vṛtta and an even-numbered pair of feet from the Prācya-vṛtta is called Pravṛttaka. When the same is formed with an even-numbered pair [of feet], it is Parāntikā. (19)
*Apārāntikā* consists of four feet with *pravṛttaka* and *yugmapāda* [metres], while *Cāruhāsinī* consists of odd-numbered feet. ||20||
When the *pravṛttaka* consists of uneven groups of four syllables (*ayugmacatuṣpāda*), it is the *cāruhāsinī*.
[These are the varieties of the *vaitālīya* meter.]
At every step in the water, his firmness was unsteady and wavering. ||21||
In each foot—meaning in every one of the four feet—the *acaladhṛti* consists of syllables devoid of heavy (*guru*) syllables;
at the end, it is a *mātrāsamaka* because of the *li* (the *la-gaṇa*, i.e., *la-la-ga*). ||22||
In each quarter there are two half-cas (ardhaca) syllables;
and when there are four cas in every quarter, with two light syllables at the end of the preceding quarter, it is *mātrāsamaka*.
O friend, if there are two cas [at the end] from the second [quarter], it is *upacitrā*. (23)
If there are four *ca*s in the quarters (*pāda*s), and a *bha* follows two *ca*s, then it is *upacitrā*. Or, if after two *ca*s there is a *kha* or a *ja*, it is *viśloka*. (24)
If there are four *ca* syllables in the quarters (*pāda*), and after the *ca* there is either *kha* or *ja*, then it is a *viśloka*;
or [it is] a *vānavāsikā* from the half-verse onward. (25)
If there are four *ca* syllables in each quarter, and after the middle [of the first half] there is either *kha* or *ja*, it is called *Vānavāsikā*;
if there is a pair of *sa*s after *ca*, it is *Citrā*. (26)
If there are four *ca* syllables in each quarter (*pāda*), followed by a *ca* and then two *sa*s, that is *citrā*.
A *kulaka* consists of quarters beginning with *mātrāsamaka*, provided they possess the characteristics described in immediate succession.
The Muni has declared the *pādākulaka* meter, which is encompassed by an unknown number of syllables per foot. ||27||

Taking at will those feet which were previously specified by their characteristics for the five types beginning with *mātrāsamaka*, that which is thus formed is *ākulaka*; its definition as *pādākulaka* was stated by Piṅgala.
Because the measure of the *vṛtta* is fixed, through such a combination, all five varieties occur in their respective order.

That [meter] which has eight and eight syllables in its two halves is called Anaṅgakrīḍā; it consists of all the other [syllables] multiplied by the oceans (four) and the Vasus (eight), with the distribution of feet arranged above. 28.
That [meter] in which there are sixteen heavy syllables (*guru*) in the first half and thirty-two light syllables (*laghu*) in the second half of every foot is called *Anaṅgakrīḍā*;
it is exceedingly beautiful, with its heavy syllables arranged at the end of each quarter-verse following ten light syllables. (29)
That [meter] in whose feet there are four *ca* syllables in both halves, with thirty light syllables and a heavy syllable at the end, is the *atirucirā*.
It is described by the sequence *ca-da-ka-da-ka-tri-caṃ ja-gi-ti*, a half-verse (*khaṇḍa*) that is unborn, devoid of *bha*, and beginningless. (30)
If in each quarter there are *ca*, *da*, *ka*, *da*, *ka*, three *jas*, and *ga*,
thus it would be a *khaṇḍa*; otherwise than what has been stated, wherever there is no *ja* [in those positions], it is the same.
Furthermore, that which exceeds the first group and is elsewhere devoid of the letter *bha*—
namely, *cadaka*, *dakatrikaṃ*, *jagiti*, *khaṇḍamajaṃ*, and *bhara-hita-mahādime*—
is the sixth chapter.
Although the meters (*vṛtta*) have already been mentioned previously, they were not stated in their entirety, but rather according to their relative importance.
Since the totality of those meters is vast, the sixfold system beginning with the *prastāra* (the expansion chart) is now set forth for the sake of thorough understanding.

In the first [meter], all syllables are heavy; in the next, the first is heavy and the one below it is light; thereafter, they are similar to the preceding ones, with the final syllables being heavy, continuing in this manner in the *prastāra* until all syllables are light. ||1||
The Paingala-prastāra.
In the procedure for constructing the *prastāra*, one should first write a meter consisting entirely of heavy syllables (*sarvaguru*).
Then, beneath the first heavy syllable, place a light syllable (*laghu*),
while the others remain identical [to those above].

The three types [of breaths], beginning with "the eastern cows," should be performed as appropriate. These too should be performed until the entire movement has become light. Among the heavy [breaths], that which is at the beginning is the eldest heavy [breath].
Below that, one should write "light" (laghu).
Then, the subsequent [syllables] are like the first; the preceding [syllable] is heavy (guru).
Thus is the Paiṅgala prastāra.
In the *prastāra*, the *paṅkti* is doubled in length; each subsequent *praticchanda* increases successively by double the number of *gaṇas* consisting of heavy and light syllables. ||2||
This is our diagrammatic arrangement (prastāra).
In the process of constructing the *prastāra*, a heavy syllable (*guru*) should be written above and a light syllable (*laghu*) below;
thus, one syllable constitutes a meter.

Having first multiplied the established number by its own value to determine the length for each meter, the preceding row increases successively by doubling the immediately following heavy and light syllables.
This is our *prastāra* (metrical array).

To determine what the *vṛtta* (meter) at this specific position is, one should place [the numbers] and then halve them according to their results; if the position is odd, one should add one before halving it.
Here, in the case of an even position, a *la* (light syllable) results; thus the "lost" [syllable] is determined. (3)
When one wishes to ask about a single uneven *vṛtta*,
then this is the rule:
such a configuration would result in this many [syllables].
For example, when it is asked how a *daśavṛtta* occurs within a four-syllable meter,
one should immediately write down ten and divide them until the remainder is lost;
"division" (*dala*) here means halving.
In that regard, wherever there is an uneven [number of syllables], one should place a single [syllable] there, making it even, and then divide it;
the meaning is that by the rule "ga iha," a guru is obtained on an uneven syllable. By the rule "same laḥ," however, a *laghu* (short) is obtained on an even syllable.
Whatever [number] is obtained, one should write each of those individually across the line;
thus, what has arisen bears fruit,
while what is lost is the "eye" (the zero).
One should write the number of this meter here in the city [of the grid] in the sequence of doubling starting from one;
however, in that case, the indicated [meter] is the one corresponding to the number of the odd-numbered pile of short syllables plus one. (4)

When it is known which position (*katitham*) a given *vṛtta* occupies by its own nature, yet it is not known what kind of *vṛtta* it is, the method for determining that (*uddiṣṭividhi*) is as follows: For example, when asked "Which *vṛtta* is this in a four-syllable meter (*caturakṣarachandaḥ*) where there are two heavy syllables (*guru*) in the middle?",
one should write the figure of that very *vṛtta* below a line and, above the line, write the numbers in sequence starting from one, each doubled in order, corresponding to the positions passed.
By this, that should be clearly stated:
there, whatever number is above the small [digits], one should add one to that in the heap above the small [digit].
By performing it in this manner, the number obtained should be understood as the indicated [result] by this much.
Here, there is one light syllable above and eight;
these together make nine,
and with the additional one, ten.
By this, the knowledge that "that event is the tenth" would arise.
This is the rule for the enumeration (uddiṣṭividhi).
Having placed the form (rūpa), one should rise by means of throws equal to the number of syllables (rasa) above the level.
The *vṛtta* [meter] consists of long and short syllables, such as one long or one short, arranged in rising sequences that gradually diminish. 5.
The Paiṅgalī Laghukriyā.

In this Vedic prosody, when one wishes to know how many meters have more than one light syllable (*laghu*), how many have exactly one light syllable, how many have two light syllables, and so forth, then the "light-syllable operation" (*laghukriyā*) is applied.

The term "form" (rūpa) has a single meaning; in that regard, having first placed one [unit] below, one should rise up sequentially above it, and the syllables should proceed in equal number, level with their respective bases and stacked one above the other.
For example, in a meter of four syllables, there are four [syllables].
By this, there would be five [combinations] for each; therein, one is a single-arising (ekotthāna) and four are four-place (catussthāna).
In the intervals between the light-arisings (laghukṛtotthāna), there are three places (tristhāna) in succession.
In two places and one place, and so on until the completion of the task; one, two, three, and so forth, up to that limit, one should write along the side.
If one asks, "What would be the accomplishment?
it is one [foot] with no light syllables,
and one [foot] with four light syllables.
There are six with two short syllables,
four with three short syllables, and one consisting entirely of short syllables.
Just as there is a light operation (*laghukriyā*), so too is there a heavy operation (*gurukriyā*);
therefore, even a meter with one heavy syllable and so forth should be understood [by this method].
Thus ends the *paiṅgalī laghukriyā*.
Having set aside the first form even before it has been assigned a number, one should then write [the numbers] below;
by mixing each with its own respective lower [value], there arise the meters *vṛtta*, *maladhva*, *ekaladhva*, and so forth.
This is my brief composition.
First, one should draw the form.
Regarding the statement, "Even when not performed, it is a light task," this refers to the meter consisting of the single syllable *e*.
By the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that it is also [a light task] when performed.
Then, having set aside the initial form and placed it aside, one should write the number of syllables of the meter in its place.

For example: in the case of a one-syllable meter and a two-syllable meter, having set aside that same initial form, one should write the number in its place. Having likewise written the number for the three-syllable meter, one should then take the "two" situated below that and combine it with the one directly beneath it.
In the same way, one should write the number for the four syllables;
then, one should mix the three situated below with the single unit of each respective triad below them.
This is our "easy method" (laghukriyā).

What is the number of syllables in the meters? The form is the product of the Yama-factors. In the Uddiṣṭa [method], the last digit is doubled, and there is also the sum of the light-syllable operations.
When it is thus desired to know how many meters (*vṛtta*) there are in this prosody, there are three methods. For example: having set down the form in four syllables, one should double it four times;
or else, according to the method of *uddiṣṭa*, the numbers are one, two, [three, etc.]...
Four and eight;
at their end, one should make the eight doubled.
Or else, having performed the light rite (laghukriyā),...
Among those, one, four, six, and four and one are to be combined.
By this, the meters (vṛtta) would be sixteenfold;
such is the number of meters. That very number multiplied by the syllables (varṇa), then its half, and then the sum of both.
First are the syllables, in the middle are the heavy [syllables], and after that are the light [syllables] and the morae. ||8||
Here, by the word *varṇa*, vowels that are not fixed among the consonants are called *akṣaras*.
This rule applies when one desires to know the number of syllables (*vṛttākṣara*) and so forth.
For example, if there are sixteen varieties of a meter consisting of four syllables, this very number written at the beginning is to be multiplied by the four syllables.
Beyond that, half of that [is the next], and beyond that as well, both together form a single unit.

There are sixty-four syllables (*akṣara*), thirty-two heavy and light syllables (*guru-laghu*), and ninety-six morae (*mātrā*). Among these, there are first sixty-four syllables; in the middle, there are also thirty-two heavy and light syllables.
But first, there are ninety-six measures;
this is the count of syllables, heavy and light syllables, and measures.
The horizontal and downward paths consist of twice the number of phonemes minus one.
For the ground for heavy and light [offenses], as well as for those in between, is indeed equal. ||9||
In this context, regarding the inquiry as to how large the *prastāra* of the meters is,
and how far it extends horizontally and vertically,
there is this rule: for example, in the case of four syllables, that group of four syllables, when doubled and multiplied by seven minus one, results in [the total number].
Therefore, even a barley-corn (*yava*) or a finger-breadth (*aṅguli*) is a transverse path (*tiryag-adhvan*).
These sixteen circles, when doubled, would amount to twenty-nine.
Consequently, a barley-corn, a finger-breadth, and so forth, constitute a downward path of thirty-one units.
In this manner, as many heavy units (gurubhūmi) as there are, so many light units (laghubhūmi) should be conceived.
As many lines as there are, so many intervals between them.
Thus, in due order, the expansion (prastāra), the lost (naṣṭa), and the indicated (uddiṣṭa) procedures for light units are established.
Number, as well as the application of time-periods—these six are the suffixes applied to past participles (vṛtta). 10.
The six [types of] meters beginning with *prastāra* are indicators for even (*samavṛtta*) meters,
not for half-even (*ardhasama*) or uneven (*viṣama*) meters.
Nor [do they exist] in the births, because that would be illogical.
If it is asked, "How then are those conditions?"
Thus, since a condition is not perceived through a slight distinction,
even the superior knowledge of the authors of treatises is correctly perceived,
just as by astronomers such as Rāhucaraṇa and others in the field of astrology.
In all prosodic expansions (*sarvaprastāra*) of even meters (*samavṛtta*), six conditions (*pratyaya*) have been stated.
Now, the knowledge of the number of heavy syllables (*guru*), light syllables (*laghu*), syllables (*akṣara*), and morae (*mātrā*) for each specific type of meter (*jāti*) is being explained.
Herein are two verses as examples:

Victorious are those—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—who are the supreme ultimate reality, who abide on the path that leads to the fruit of all ultimate goals, and who are the persons produced thereby. || 1 ||
Victorious is the Jina, who has realized the Dharma; victorious is his companion, Prajñā;
and victorious is the assembly of noble ones, whose bodies are the fruit of the seed of liberation consisting of skillful means and the rest. || 2 ||
In this [meter], there are fifty-seven mātrās,
forty syllables,
and seventeen long syllables.
There are twenty-three *laghu*s.
Having shown these two numbers, because the others become clear accordingly, they (*mātrā*s) should be observed at the end of the placement procedure (*nyāsakarman*) both below and above the *agha*.
The *mātrā*s of those devoid of *laghu* syllables, when deprived of *laghu*s, constitute their half.
And just as the morae are devoid of phonemes, so too are there that many heavy syllables here. (11)
When asked: "There are 40 syllables (varṇas) and 57 morae (mātrās); there are 23 short syllables (laghus). How many long syllables (gurus) are there? [the answer is as follows].
They should be joined at the beginning and the end;
having placed them in the middle, they should be split.
By this, there will be seventeen *gurus*.
The number of gurus.

The quantity [of time] is twice as great as the heavy syllables; the syllables are devoid of quantity, yet their letters are doubled. And the letters are devoid of heaviness, for just as many light syllables exist here.
Mātrās: 57, syllables (varṇas): 40; syllables: 40, heavy syllables (gurus): 17; mātrās: 57, heavy syllables: 17. Having doubled the heavy syllables at the beginning, one should add the mātrās.
Having doubled the syllables in the middle, one should join them with the appropriate prosodic measure (mātrā), and at the end, one should join the heavy syllables (gurus).
By this means, there will be twenty-three light syllables (laghus).
The small number.

As many as are the sums of heavy and light syllables, as many as are the morae (mātrās) excluding the heavy syllables, and as many as are half the sum of the light syllables—in this [system], there are that many syllables. 13.
Seventeen *gurus*, fifty-seven *mātrās*, fifty-seven *mātrās*, twenty-three *laghus*, seventeen *gurus*, and twenty-three *laghus* should be placed at the beginning.
It should be joined in the middle and split at the end;
by this, there are forty syllables.
The number of syllables.

The number of syllables, when doubled and subtracted by the number of light syllables, and likewise the number of syllables mixed with heavy syllables, results in exactly that many morae (mātrās) here. 14.

There are 23 short syllables (laghu), 40 vowels (varṇa), 40 vowels, 17 long syllables (guru), 23 short syllables, and 17 long syllables; having doubled the number of long syllables at the beginning, they should be set down.
In the middle, the syllables should be doubled; the short vowels should be joined; and at the end, they should be mixed.
By this, there would be fifty-seven mātrās;
such is the count of mātrās.
Whatever merit has been born for me from propitiating this knowledge of the Jina, may the supreme ones of the world, through that [merit], propitiate this knowledge. (15)
(Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Chandoratnākara* composed by Ratnākaraśānti.
The work titled *Chandoratnākara*, the composition of the venerable Ratnākaraśānti, the omniscient one of the Kali Age, is hereby completed.
May there be auspiciousness for all the world!
This is the work of the venerable Śāntipāda, the ocean of jewels and omniscient one of the Kali age.
It was written by the Śākya bhikṣu Dharmapālabhadra, the foremost jewel among the eyes of the world.
Furthermore, it was composed for Jaṅchupacemo (Bodhiśekhara), who is called the incomparable great protector of the three worlds.

Furthermore, based on the words of those [previous] feet and relying upon the permission granted by that very same teacher, who was protected by compassion for virtuous beings, the illustrious Bhikṣu Nam-mkha’-bsam-pa (Ratnadharmapālabhadra) revised it.
May this also benefit all sentient beings through the jewel of the Buddha’s teaching.
The *Chandoratnākara*, the work of the venerable Śānti, the ocean of jewels and omniscient one of the Kali age, is hereby completed.
This was translated by the Dharma-holder Rasavāyaraluṅgapā Ṅagpa Gyalachena (Kīrtidhvaja).
Furthermore, it was [revised] by Jaṅchupacemo (Bodhiśekhara) for the sake of the incomparable Great Omniscient One of the Three Worlds, Abhihitābhidhāna.

Furthermore, based on the oral instructions of that very same master, the monk Namakhā-saṅpo (Ākāśabhadra)— a Śākya bhikṣu protected by the compassion of the virtuous, adorned with the crest-jewel of supreme restraint and diligence, and the sole sovereign among those who have mastered the single treatise of the Tripiṭaka— the illustrious Lo-chen-sten-pa (Sthiramati) transcribed it from the original manuscript into the Indian script; it was then translated and edited at the great monastic center of Śrī Ewaṃ.
